kjv-italics-revision.d: Open a King James Bible. Some words are printed in italics. Those are words the 1611 translators added to make the English read smoothly. They are not in the Hebrew.
Nobody translating from ancient gold plates could know which English words a 1611 committee had added. Those words exist only in that one edition.

kjv-italics-revision.t: What the Book of Mormon does
kjv-italics-revision.d: It quotes long stretches of Isaiah. Where its wording differs from the King James, the changes cluster on exactly those italic words. David Wright counted it: between 22% and 38% of the differences land there. And about 40% of the italic words are simply dropped.

Stan Spencer of the Interpreter Foundation accepts the pattern. He argues Joseph Smith could see the italics on the page, treated them as suspect, and revised around them while dictating. That is a real answer, and it fits the data.
It concedes he was working from a King James Bible. That is the whole point at issue.
"Why would a translation from gold plates track the italics of one English edition?"

deutero-isaiah-problem.d: Most scholars think Isaiah 40-55 had a second, unnamed author. They date it to about 545 BC, during the exile in Babylon. Two reasons. Those chapters treat the exile as already happening. And they name Cyrus, a Persian king who had not been born in Isaiah's day.

deutero-isaiah-problem.t: Why that is a problem here
deutero-isaiah-problem.d: Lehi left Jerusalem around 600 BC, before the exile. So those chapters could not have been on the brass plates he carried. Yet Nephi, Jacob and Abinadi all quote them at length.

Two lines. Kevin Barney and FAIR accept the late dating. They suggest the wording entered during translation — Joseph putting Nephite ideas into the King James Isaiah he knew. Others reject the dating and defend one Isaiah in the 700s BC.

Strong for you. The first answer concedes that part of the text is not ancient. The second requires overturning two centuries of scholarship — which some conservatives do attempt, and you should say so.
"If those chapters were written after Lehi left, how were they on his plates?"

another-gospel-canon-closure.t: The two verses Christians reach for
another-gospel-canon-closure.d: Galatians 1:8 — "though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you… let him be accursed" — applied to the angel Moroni. And Revelation 22:18, warning against adding to the book.

another-gospel-canon-closure.t: Be careful with the second one
another-gospel-canon-closure.d: Revelation 22:18 says "the words of the prophecy of this book." That means Revelation itself. It is a standard closing curse for one ancient scroll. Revelation was not even the last book of the New Testament written. Using it to shut the whole Bible is bad reading, and your friend will say so.

another-gospel-canon-closure.t: Where the first verse does work
another-gospel-canon-closure.d: Galatians 1:8 is different. It does not say an angel cannot appear. It grants the possibility and removes its authority: the message is tested by the gospel already delivered. And Paul includes himself — though we — which makes it a test rather than a weapon.
Arguable both ways. The canon half fails. The Galatians half holds — and it holds against us too.
"I'd have to reject an angel with a new gospel too. Paul puts himself under that rule."

grace-after-all-we-can-do.d: 2 Nephi 25:23 — "it is by grace that we are saved, after all we can do." Moroni 10:32 adds: deny yourselves of all ungodliness, then is his grace sufficient.
It reads like a condition. Your own maximum effort first, then God covers the gap. Ephesians 2:8-9 says the opposite — saved by grace through faith, "not of works, lest any man should boast."

Stephen Robinson of BYU says "after all we can do" is an old turn of phrase. He reads it as in spite of all we can do. And in 2015 Dieter Uchtdorf, of the First Presidency, preached grace in words most evangelicals would recognise.

Arguable both ways. The old-phrase reading is fair. The modern preaching is real. But ask what the system asks of a member in practice. Temple worthiness. Interviews. Ordinances. Then see if that matches the sermon.
"When you stand before God, what are you resting on?"

trinitarian-monotheism-1830.t: What the Book of Mormon says about God
trinitarian-monotheism-1830.d: It is strictly monotheistic, and the Father-Son unity is so tight it reads almost as one person in two roles. Mosiah 15:1-5 has Christ as "the Father and the Son… one God." Alma 11:26-29 says there is one God and no other.
That the Father, Son and Holy Ghost are three separate beings. That the Father has a body of flesh and bone. And that faithful people may become gods themselves.

David Paulsen of BYU says the 1830 text read whole is not modalist. It does tell Father and Son apart in other places. He adds that early Christian writers were loose with words too, before the councils tightened them.
Arguable on any one verse. Harder to argue with is the direction of travel. The 1830 book sounds much more like ordinary Christianity than 1844 does.
"Read me Alma 11:26-29 in your own book. How many Gods does it say there are?"

1837-son-of-edits.d: 1 Nephi 11:18 called Mary "the mother of God." 11:21 called Jesus "the Lamb of God, yea, even the Eternal Father." 13:40 said "the Lamb of God is the Eternal Father."
Joseph Smith inserted the words the Son of. Mary became the mother of the Son of God. The Lamb became the Son of the Eternal Father. The change is small and it is not accidental.
FAIR says a translator may clarify his own work. Royal Skousen treats the change as clarifying, not correcting. Both readings work, they say, since Christ is called Eternal Father in the book anyway.
Arguable. But watch the timing. The edits land just as the teaching about God moves from one being to three separate ones.
"Why did those four verses need the words 'the Son of' added in 1837?"

jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132.t: What the Book of Mormon says
jacob-polygamy-vs-dc132.d: Jacob 2:24 says David's and Solomon's many wives were "abominable before me, saith the Lord." Verse 27 commands: "there shall not any man among you have save it be one wife; and concubines he shall have none."
That David's wives and concubines "were given unto him of me." The same practice, from the same God, with the opposite verdict.
FAIR points to Jacob 2:30, which they read as an exception clause: monogamy is the rule, unless God commands otherwise to raise up seed. That reading is available in the text.
Here the Bible and the Book of Mormon agree with each other, and D&C 132 stands alone against both. That is worth pointing out gently.
"Your own scripture calls it abominable. What changed?"

unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett.t: What the Book of Mormon says
unchangeable-god-vs-king-follett.d: Moroni 8:18 — God is "unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity." That matches the Bible: Psalm 90:2, Malachi 3:6, and Isaiah 43:10, where God says "before me there was no God formed."
In 1844 he preached at a funeral for a man named King Follett. He taught that God "was once as we are now" — a man who rose to become God. And that we may do the same.

Blake Ostler and FAIR argue Moroni 8:18 is about God's character — he is not fickle or partial — rather than his history. The surrounding verses are about God's fairness to children, which supports that reading.
Strong for you. The character reading is fair for Moroni 8:18 on its own. It does not help with Isaiah 43:10, which is about existence, not temperament.
"Read me Isaiah 43:10. Was there ever a God before this one?"

no-postmortem-repentance.t: What the Book of Mormon says
no-postmortem-repentance.d: Alma 34:32-35: "this life is the time for men to prepare to meet God," and after it comes "the night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed." Those who put off repentance are sealed to the devil — "this is the final state of the wicked."
The spirit world, where the gospel is preached to the dead, and baptism performed by proxy for them by the living.

That Amulek is addressing the Zoramites — people who had already received the gospel and rejected it. His warning applies to them, not to the billions who never heard. D&C 138 makes that distinction explicit.
Genuinely arguable. The Zoramite context is real. But Alma's language is sweeping, and the Bible says the same thing in Hebrews 9:27.
"Alma says there's no labour after this life. How does that fit with baptism for the dead?"

born-at-jerusalem.d: Alma 7:10 prophesies that Jesus "shall be born of Mary, at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers." The Bible says Bethlehem — Micah 5:2 predicts it, Matthew 2 and Luke 2 report it.

And this one is good. The verse says the land of our fathers, not the city. The Book of Mormon uses "the land of Jerusalem" more than forty times for the whole region. Bethlehem is five miles away. An Egyptian letter from the 1300s BC even calls Bethlehem part of the land of Jerusalem.
Genuinely arguable, and this is one where the Latter-day Saint answer is stronger than most critics admit. Do not lead with it.
Give away a weak argument openly and you earn a hearing on the strong ones. The papyri. The italics. The Isaiah dating.
"I've heard this one used against you and I don't think it works. Can I ask about something that does?"

plain-precious-things-removed.t: The claim that makes a restoration necessary
plain-precious-things-removed.d: 1 Nephi 13 says a "great and abominable church" deliberately took from the gospel "many parts which are plain and most precious, and also many covenants." If the Bible was gutted, something has to replace it.
Because we have the copies. Thousands of them, from before and across that whole span. In Greek, Latin, Syriac and Coptic. Made in places that never spoke to each other.
No sign of a coordinated removal. Variants exist and are catalogued, but they are spelling, word order, and a handful of footnoted passages. Nothing doctrine rests on.

FAIR and Scripture Central move the loss earlier — to the first or second century, before our oldest full copies. If it happened then, the copies could not show it. That is a real answer. It is also one that no evidence could ever count against.
"If it was removed before our oldest copies, what evidence could ever count either way?"

no-nephite-material-culture.d: Cities. Temples. Roads. Coins. Steel swords and armour. Civilizations in the millions. And a final battle with hundreds of thousands of dead.
After about 190 years of digging in the Americas: not one city. Not one battlefield, road, temple or skeleton tied to the book. No inscription. And no site the church itself points to.

John Sorenson keeps the whole story inside a corridor of about 500 miles in Central America. If that is right, an empty hemisphere proves nothing. He lists hundreds of claimed matches with Maya culture.

The church takes no official position on where it happened. And the small-map idea is a long way from what was taught for a century. Back then, the Lamanites were the ancestors of all American Indians.
"Where did it happen? I'd genuinely like to read the church's position on that."

translation-seer-stone.d: Joseph Smith reading from gold plates, perhaps with a curtain, writing down what he read. That is what church manuals and paintings showed for about 150 years.

Something different. He put a brown stone into his hat, buried his face in it to block the light, and dictated. The plates were often covered, or in another room, or not there at all. That comes from Emma Smith, David Whitmer and Martin Harris — insiders, not critics.
He had used the same stone earlier for treasure-seeking, which is what brought him before a court in 1826.

This one has a clear answer — the church now teaches it openly. The Gospel Topics essay says so, the Joseph Smith Papers document it, and the church published photographs of the stone in 2015. The scandal was the silence, not the stone.
"Have you seen the church's photos of the seer stone? What did you picture before that?"

lost-116-pages.d: In 1828 Martin Harris borrowed the first 116 pages of the translation and lost them. They were never recovered.

They were not retranslated. A revelation, now D&C 10, said wicked men had altered the lost pages and would publish the altered version to discredit him. So he was told to translate a different set of plates covering the same period instead.

That this is guarding against forgery, not dodging. Dictated translation never comes out word for word the same twice. If enemies held the only other copy, any difference would be paraded as proof he made it up.
Arguable. The forgery worry is reasonable. What is worth noticing is that a replacement text already existed, covering the same years. And no altered version was ever published.
"Did the altered pages ever actually appear?"

witnesses-character-and-vision.d: Eleven men signed statements printed in the front of every Book of Mormon. Three describe an angel and a voice; eight describe handling the plates. It is the strongest evidence the book has, and it deserves serious treatment.

witnesses-character-and-vision.t: What is worth knowing about them
witnesses-character-and-vision.d: All eleven were Smith family, Whitmer family, or Martin Harris. None was an outsider. And all of them lived in a world where seeing by "second sight" was normal.

witnesses-character-and-vision.t: How some of them described it
witnesses-character-and-vision.d: Harris spoke of seeing "with the eyes of faith" and "spiritual eyes." Stephen Burnett's 1838 letter reports Harris saying so publicly.

witnesses-character-and-vision.t: Their answer, and it is strong
witnesses-character-and-vision.d: Not one of the eleven ever took it back. Not Cowdery. Not Harris. Not Whitmer — even after being thrown out of the church, when taking it back would have cost nothing. Whitmer never came back to the church, and reaffirmed it as he was dying.
Genuinely arguable, and this is the best card the other side holds. Treat it with respect.
"What do you make of the 'spiritual eyes' language? I'm asking honestly."

gold-plates-never-examined.d: The plates were shown only to people Joseph Smith chose. Family. Money backers. Early believers. Then they were returned to the angel. No scholar or neutral party ever saw them, and none ever can.

gold-plates-never-examined.t: What that does and does not mean
gold-plates-never-examined.d: It is not proof of anything on its own. Plenty of genuine ancient objects are lost. But it does mean the central physical evidence for the book is permanently unavailable for testing.

An interesting one. Witnesses put the plates at 40 to 60 pounds. Solid gold that size would weigh about 200. But tumbaga is different — a copper-gold mix used in Central America, gilded on the surface. Plates that size in tumbaga would weigh about 53 to 58 pounds, and look like gold. That fits a real object better than a forger would have guessed.
Strong for you on the main point, but give them the tumbaga argument first. It is a good one, and pretending otherwise costs you.
"Is there anything that could be examined today, either way?"

kinderhook-plates.d: In 1843 three men in Illinois made six small brass plates. They covered them in made-up "ancient" writing, buried them in a mound, and brought them to Joseph Smith. The point was to see whether he would translate them.

His clerk William Clayton recorded that Smith said the plates contained the history of a descendant of Ham. The plates were later proved a hoax; one of the makers admitted it, and metal testing in 1980 confirmed a nineteenth-century origin.

And the church's own published position agrees with much of it. Smith never produced a translation. He never claimed revelation about them. Don Bradley and Mark Ashurst-McGee argue he was trying a scholarly comparison, using his Egyptian alphabet papers.
This one has a clear answer, and the answer goes largely their way. Clayton's entry is secondhand, and no translation exists. Use it as evidence about method, not as a knockout.
"What do you make of the Kinderhook episode? I've read the church's account of it."

source-parallels-voth-late-war.t: Two books that were around before 1830
source-parallels-voth-late-war.d: Ethan Smith's View of the Hebrews (1823) argued American Indians descended from the lost tribes of Israel. It was published in the town where Oliver Cowdery's family lived. And Gilbert Hunt's The Late War (1816) retold the War of 1812 in King James English for schoolchildren.

B. H. Roberts, a senior Latter-day Saint leader and historian, privately compiled a 291-page study listing about 26 structural similarities with View of the Hebrews — a divided people, a buried record, and more.

Roberts drew no conclusion of dependence. He framed the work as questions a believer must be able to answer, and he died affirming the Book of Mormon. Using him as a witness for the prosecution misrepresents what he said.
Genuinely arguable. Parallels are easy to find and easy to overstate. The honest version is narrow: these ideas were in the air, in that region, in that decade.
"Have you read what B. H. Roberts actually wrote? He was one of yours."

book-of-abraham-papyri.t: Why this case is different from all the others
book-of-abraham-papyri.d: The source document survives. For the Book of Mormon the plates are gone. Here, we have the papyri.

In 1835 Joseph Smith bought Egyptian papyri from a travelling mummy exhibition. He declared one roll to be "the writings of Abraham while he was in Egypt" and published the Book of Abraham in 1842. The papyri were thought lost, then rediscovered in 1966.

book-of-abraham-papyri.t: What they turned out to be
book-of-abraham-papyri.d: Ordinary Egyptian funeral texts. A Book of Breathings, made for a Theban priest named Hor, from about the second century BC. That is roughly 1,500 years after Abraham. Every Egyptologist who has looked at them agrees, including Latter-day Saint ones.

Two defences, both in the church's own essay. The missing-scroll idea says the surviving pieces are a small remnant. The Abraham text was on a part now lost. The catalyst idea says the papyri only prompted revelation. On that view the words were never on them at all.
Strong for you — this is the single most testable claim in the whole section. But note what the catalyst theory concedes: that the words are not on the papyri at all.
"The church says Egyptologists read these differently than he did. What do you make of that?"

stylometry-wordprint-studies.d: Writers have measurable habits — how often they use small words like of and and. Statisticians have tried to use those fingerprints to work out who wrote the Book of Mormon.

BYU studies by Larsen, Rencher and Layton (1980) and Hilton (1990) found the book's internal narrators are statistically distinguishable from each other and from Joseph Smith. Jockers, Witten and Criddle (2008) pointed instead toward Sidney Rigdon and Solomon Spalding.

BYU statistician Bruce Schaalje identified it. The Jockers method is a closed-set classifier: it is mathematically obliged to assign every chapter to one of the candidates you feed it. If the real author is not on the list, it will still return a confident answer.
Genuinely arguable, and honestly neither side settles anything. Do not cite either study as proof — the method is contested enough that both results should be held loosely.
Nothing. This is a case to know about so you don't get caught using it.

jst-genesis-50-choice-seer.t: What Joseph Smith added to Genesis
jst-genesis-50-choice-seer.d: He produced a revision of the whole Bible. In his version, Genesis 50 gains about fourteen verses in which the dying Joseph of Egypt prophesies a latter-day "choice seer" who will be named Joseph — and whose father will also be named Joseph.
Joseph Smith Jr. His father was Joseph Smith Sr.
Nothing like it. Not the Hebrew. Not the Dead Sea Scrolls. Not the Greek. Not the Samaritan text. No ancient copy of Genesis has these verses.

Robert Matthews and Kent Jackson agree that no manuscript has the passage. They argue the revision was never meant to be pure restoration of lost text. It could be new revelation, or inspired comment, added to the page.
Strong for you. That answer is honest, and it concedes the point: a prophecy naming the translator was inserted into Genesis by the translator.
"Which ancient manuscript has those verses in Genesis 50?"

angel-nephi-moroni-name-change.d: Every Latter-day Saint knows him as Moroni — the last Nephite, who buried the plates and returned as an angel to reveal them.

Joseph Smith's official history, published in the Times and Seasons in April 1842 under his own editorship, names the angel Nephi. So does the Millennial Star the same year, the first edition of the Pearl of Great Price in 1851, and Lucy Mack Smith's 1853 history.

FAIR and church historians call it a copying slip. They say clerks introduced it while compiling the 1838-39 history. And they point to earlier sources that already say Moroni — Oliver Cowdery's letters from 1835.
Genuinely arguable. A clerical error is entirely possible. What makes it worth knowing is that the error survived into published scripture and stood for years.
"Have you seen the 1842 Times and Seasons? It names the angel Nephi."

first-vision-multiple-accounts.d: God the Father and Jesus Christ appearing to Joseph Smith in a grove of trees. Everything else rests on it.

first-vision-multiple-accounts.t: He told it more than once
first-vision-multiple-accounts.d: At least four times in his own lifetime, and the accounts differ. The 1832 one is in his own handwriting. It describes one person, not two. It gives his age as about fifteen or sixteen. And it says he had already decided the churches were wrong before he prayed. The 1838 account — the one now in scripture — has two persons and a different order of events.

The church's own Gospel Topics essay acknowledges all the accounts. It argues the differences reflect audience, purpose and memory rather than invention: the 1832 telling is about personal forgiveness, the 1838 about which church to join.

Genuinely arguable. People do retell formative experiences differently. What is harder is that the number of persons present changes, and that most members never heard there was more than one account.
"Have you read the 1832 account in his own hand? The church published it."

first-vision-revival-dating.d: That there was an "unusual excitement on the subject of religion" in the Palmyra area in 1820, which added "great multitudes" to the churches, and that this is what sent him to pray.

Wesley Walters went looking in 1967. He examined Presbyterian, Methodist and Baptist records for Palmyra and found no significant revival in 1820. The major local revival was in 1824-25 — after the date given.

Milton Backman replied in 1969, documenting Methodist camp meetings near Palmyra in 1819-20 and revival activity across the wider Genesee region. "In that region of country" is a loose phrase and need not mean Palmyra alone.
Genuinely arguable. Backman's reply is real and should be given. But the account describes multitudes joining churches locally, and the membership numbers for those years do not show it.
"When was the big revival in Palmyra? It's worth checking the church records."

word-of-wisdom-dietary-law.d: D&C 89, given in 1833. It counsels against wine, strong drink, tobacco and "hot drinks" — later defined as coffee and tea. Its own second verse says it is sent "not by commandment or constraint."
Under Heber J. Grant, keeping it became a fixed requirement for a temple recommend, formalised by about 1921. So a cup of coffee can now keep a member out of the temple, and out of a child's wedding.
That it is a health code and a covenant standard, not a purity law — the body as a temple, as in 1 Corinthians 6:19-20. A church may raise a standard over time without contradicting itself.
Arguable both ways. The real question is not coffee. It is what happens when advice given expressly not as a commandment becomes a test of worthiness. That is close to what Jesus rebuked in Mark 7.
"D&C 89:2 says it isn't a commandment. When did that change, and who changed it?"

temple-garments-practice.d: Endowed members covenant to wear the temple garment — prescribed white underclothing bearing sacred marks. The General Handbook instructs that it be worn "day and night throughout your life" and never altered. Since 2024 the recommend interview includes a standard statement about it.
Do not mock it. "Magic underwear" is the single fastest way to end the conversation, and it deserves to end. This is sacred to the person in front of you and it is personal.
That it is a private reminder of covenants made in the temple — no stranger than a nun's habit, a priest's collar, a Jewish prayer shawl or a Muslim skullcap. That comparison is fair.
Not whether clothing can be sacred — plainly it can. Whether daily clothing should be a condition of standing before God, and where Scripture prescribes that for ordinary believers.
"I'm not going to make fun of it. Can I ask what it means to you?"

kjv-isaiah-block-quotation.t: What is actually in the book
kjv-isaiah-block-quotation.d: About 21 chapters of Isaiah sit inside the Book of Mormon. They are in 1 Nephi 20-21, 2 Nephi 7-8, 2 Nephi 12-24, 2 Nephi 27, Mosiah 14 and 3 Nephi 22. The wording is almost identical to the King James Version.
The King James Version is an English translation from 1611. Lehi left Jerusalem around 600 BC. A fresh translation from his brass plates should not match one later English edition word for word.

Royal Skousen is the leading Latter-day Saint scholar of the text. His critical work found the quotations match later King James printings. Not even the 1611 original. And where the Book of Mormon does differ, the changes rarely give a better Hebrew reading.

FAIR and Skousen say the translation was never word for word. Where the plates matched the Bible, the familiar King James wording was supplied. Either Joseph consulted a Bible, or revelation gave him King James style English. Skousen adds that some variants look like older English streams rather than copying.
Strong for you. Their own leading textual scholar concedes where the English came from. The answer explains the dependence. It does not deny it.
"Why does it track a later King James printing rather than the Hebrew?"

kjv-translation-errors-copied.t: What a translation error looks like
kjv-translation-errors-copied.d: The 1611 translators got some Hebrew words wrong. Those mistakes belong to their English. They are not in the Hebrew text at all.

2 Nephi 14:5 has "upon all the glory shall be a defence." The Hebrew word there, chuppah, means canopy. 2 Nephi 21:3 has "make him of quick understanding," where the Hebrew says his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. And 2 Nephi 16:2 keeps the King James double plurals seraphims and cherubims. Hebrew already makes those words plural.
These are marks of one English committee's work in 1611. A translation made from a Hebrew source would not carry them.

FAIR says a translation aimed at King James readers may keep familiar wording even where it is imperfect. Some of the disputed lines are defensible readings of ambiguous Hebrew. And D&C 1:24 says God speaks to people after the manner of their language. So the errors sit in the English layer, not on the plates.
Strong for you. The King James artifacts are granted. The defence moves them into a translation convention. And no variant anywhere pulls the wording back toward the Hebrew.
"If the Hebrew word means canopy, why does your book say defence?"

sermon-on-mount-3-nephi.d: 3 Nephi 12-14 gives the Sermon on the Mount to the Nephites. It is near-verbatim King James English, matching Matthew 5-7.

Eight places where 3 Nephi follows late Greek manuscripts that scholars judge to be later additions. The clearest is the close of the Lord's Prayer at 3 Nephi 13:13 — "For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, forever." That line is missing from the earliest copies of Matthew 6:13. The word openly at 3 Nephi 13:4, 6 and 18 is the same kind of case.
A record of Jesus speaking in the New World should not follow scribal additions made between the 300s and the 1500s.

John Welch of BYU answered at length. Several of Larson's eight are text-critically uncertain rather than settled. And one runs the other way. 3 Nephi 12:22 drops "without a cause," agreeing with the earliest manuscripts against the King James. Welch also points to deliberate changes for the Nephite setting, which mechanical copying would not produce.
Genuinely arguable. Welch's without a cause point is real, and you should hand it over before anyone asks. The doxology and openly are still best explained by King James dependence.
"Why does the Nephite sermon include a line the earliest copies of Matthew don't have?"

nt-phrasing-in-preexilic-books.t: What is in the early books
nt-phrasing-in-preexilic-books.d: Books set between 600 and 100 BC are full of New Testament wording. 2 Nephi 4:17 has "O wretched man that I am," which is Romans 7:24. 2 Nephi 9:39 has "to be carnally-minded is death," which is Romans 8:6. 1 Nephi 22:20 quotes Peter's version of Deuteronomy 18 from Acts 3:22-23. Alma 5:52 echoes John the Baptist in Matthew 3:10.
Moroni 7:45-47 tracks 1 Corinthians 13:4-8 almost word for word. Moroni 10:8-17 does the same with 1 Corinthians 12:4-11.
Nicholas Frederick, a BYU professor, has catalogued roughly 650 New Testament phrases woven through the text. That number comes from inside the church.

FAIR and Frederick both say the New Testament language belongs to the translation, not the plates. Joseph, or a revealed translation aimed at 1820s Bible readers, put Nephite ideas into the scriptural English they knew. Some parallels may also come from shared Old World sources, or from the same gospel being revealed twice.

Strong for you. The fact is granted at BYU. The translation-idiom answer concedes that the English is not a literal rendering of an ancient record. And it strains hardest where a whole sermon is built on a New Testament passage.
"How does a prophet writing before Christ quote Paul?"

hebrews-in-alma-12-13.d: A sermon dated to about 82 BC. It is about priesthood "after the order of the Son," about Melchizedek, and about entering God's "rest."

That the sermon reproduces the argument sequence, the interpretive moves and the King James wording of Hebrews 3:7-4:11 and 7:1-4. Alma 13:17-19 tracks Hebrews 7:1-4 closely. Scholars treat that Hebrews material as the author's own fusion of Genesis 14 and Psalm 110. No pre-Christian source contains it.

John Welch and the FARMS reviewers say both texts could draw on older Melchizedek traditions. Those traditions do exist: 11QMelchizedek and the Genesis Apocryphon, both from the Dead Sea Scrolls. They add that the shared wording is translation register. And Alma's emphasis differs — repentance and ordination, rather than Christ's superiority. Copying would not produce that.

Genuinely arguable. Wright's verbal case has not been taken apart. But the shared-tradition answer is a real alternative, even though no manuscript supports it directly. The parallels favour Wright. They do not close it.
"Which older source has the Melchizedek argument Alma 13 uses?"

mark-long-ending-mormon-9.d: Mormon 9:22-24 has the risen Jesus commissioning the Nephite disciples. The words are nearly identical to Mark 16:15-18 in the King James. Ether 4:18 uses the same material.
Mark 16:9-20 is called the long ending. It is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Most textual scholars judge it a second-century addition.

Book of Mormon Central's KnoWhy 522 gives two lines. First, a minority of credentialed scholars outside the church defend the long ending as authentic — Nicholas Lunn and James Snapp, on patristic and internal grounds. Second, even if it is a later addition, Moroni was quoting the Nephite record. The risen Lord could give the same commission in both hemispheres.
Genuinely arguable, and the second answer is hard to disprove. Lunn and Snapp are real scholars with published defences. But they are a minority. On the majority view the problem stands.
"Do you know the story behind the last twelve verses of Mark?"

horses-anachronism.d: Horses among the Jaredites and Nephites, from about 2500 BC to AD 400. Some are harnessed to chariots. See 1 Nephi 18:25, Enos 1:21, Alma 18:9-12, 3 Nephi 3:22 and Ether 9:19.

Horses died out in the Americas around 10,000 BC. The Spanish brought them back in the 1500s. In between there are no verified remains, no pictures and no words for them. The same blank covers cattle, oxen, asses, swine, and the elephants of Ether 9:19.

Book of Mormon Central and FAIR give three lines. Horse may be a loanshift — a familiar word used for a native animal such as a deer or a tapir. Spaniards and native peoples did exactly that with unfamiliar animals. Small groups of horses may also have survived unnoticed; Wade Miller has had candidate remains tested. And bones rot fast in tropical soil.

No verified pre-Columbian horse has been produced. Tested candidates came back either Ice Age or after Columbus. The loanshift answer concedes that no actual horses were there. And it strains at the chariots, which need a draught animal.
Strong for you, but give the loanshift answer first and give it fairly. Michael Coe, a Yale archaeologist, laid the problem out in Dialogue in 1973.
"Has one pre-Columbian horse bone ever dated to Book of Mormon times?"

steel-and-ferrous-metallurgy.d: Nephi's "bow of steel" carried from Arabia. Nephites teaching people to make steel and to work "in all manner of iron," around 590 to 400 BC. And Jaredite steel swords at Ether 7:9.
The Old World half and the New World half are different arguments. Keep them apart. One of them is answered and one is not.

steel-and-ferrous-metallurgy.t: The Old World half is answered
steel-and-ferrous-metallurgy.d: A carburised steel sword was dug up at Vered Jericho in Israel, dated about 620 BC. It is in the Israel Museum. So real steel existed in Lehi's Jerusalem. Concede that plainly.

Archaeology finds no iron working anywhere in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica. No smelting sites, no slag, no tools, no iron or steel weapons. Metalwork of any kind shows up only around AD 600 to 800, and it never included smelting iron.

FAIR notes that steel in King James English can mean any hardened metal; the King James uses it for Hebrew bronze. Mesoamericans did work meteoric iron. And a small Nephite industry might leave little trace. Michael Coe and Deanne Matheny have both pressed the other way.
"I'll grant you Laban's sword. What about the iron industry in America?"

wheat-barley-silk.d: Nephites and Jaredites growing wheat and barley, and producing silk. See Mosiah 9:9, Alma 1:29, Ether 9:17 and Ether 10:24.
Old World wheat, barley and silkworm farming are absent from the pre-Columbian record. Farming in the Americas ran on maize, beans and squash.

wheat-barley-silk.t: One point in their favour first
wheat-barley-silk.d: Barley is built into the measures at Alma 11:7 and 11:15. Those are weights, not coins. The word coins was a twentieth-century chapter heading, and the church has since corrected it. Do not repeat the coins version.

Domesticated little barley, Hordeum pusillum, has since been confirmed as a cultivated grain in pre-Columbian North America. Nobody knew that in 1830. So barley is no longer a clean anachronism. FAIR defends wheat and silk as loanshifts too. A familiar word could stand for a native grain such as amaranth. Or for fine local fibres like kapok, and the wild-silk cloth attested in Mesoamerica.

Genuinely arguable, and lopsided. The little-barley find is a real point for them, and wild silk is attested. Old World wheat is still unattested anywhere. And the loanshift answer again grants that the named thing was not there. Michael Coe set out the original problem.
"The barley one has a real answer. Where does the wheat come from?"

greek-names-timothy-lachoneus.d: Greek personal names in a Hebrew colony. Timothy and Jonas at 3 Nephi 19:4. Lachoneus at 3 Nephi 1:1, a name meaning the Laconian. And the risen Jesus calling himself "Alpha and Omega" at 3 Nephi 9:18.
Alpha and omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. The phrase comes from Revelation 1:8. A colony that left Jerusalem in 600 BC and wrote in reformed Egyptian had no Greek contact.

Hugh Nibley and Stephen Ricks point to real history. From the mid-600s BC, Ionian and Carian mercenaries and traders served in Egypt, including in Necho II's army, and moved across the Levant. Greek names could reach Lehi's people, or more easily the Mulekites. They add that Timothy, Jonas and "Alpha and Omega" may be the translator's English stand-ins for Nephite equivalents.

Genuinely arguable, and this is a small case. The mercenary history is real. Substitution works well for "Alpha and Omega." Lachoneus as a personal name, and the exact match with Revelation, still fit an 1829 writer more easily. Grant Palmer made that case.
"Where would a Nephite have picked up the Greek alphabet?"

church-bible-synagogue-terms.d: Church, used of Jerusalem in 600 BC at 1 Nephi 4:26. It is used of formal Nephite bodies too. Synagogues, at 2 Nephi 26:26 and Alma 16:13. Those did not exist until after the exile. And the word Bible, on Nephi's lips at 2 Nephi 29:3-10.

church-bible-synagogue-terms.t: Why the third one is different
church-bible-synagogue-terms.d: The word Bible comes from the Greek biblia. It was first used for the bound book long after Christ. And that passage answers an 1830s objection in its own words: "A Bible! A Bible! We have got a Bible."

FAIR says the first two are just the translator's English. He had to call Nephite meetings something. The King James is loose with church too. Lee Levine, who studies synagogues, allows for shared worship before the exile in the gate chambers. And Bible sits inside a prophecy about the last days. Knowing a future thing is the point of it.

Weak on the first two words. Worth a look on the third. Any translator uses his own words for groups and buildings. So do not press those two. 2 Nephi 29 is different. It argues with critics who were not yet born.
"Who is Nephi arguing with in 2 Nephi 29?"

dark-skin-curse.d: 2 Nephi 5:21 says God cursed the Lamanites with "a skin of blackness," so they would not be "enticing" to the Nephites. Alma 3:6-9 marks their descendants. 3 Nephi 2:14-15 has converted Lamanites becoming white. Jacob 3:8-9 and Mormon 5:15 belong with these.

Acts 17:26 says God made all nations "of one blood." Acts 10:34-35 says he shows no partiality. 1 Samuel 16:7 says he looks on the heart. Galatians 3:28, John 7:24 and Revelation 7:9 point the same way.

dark-skin-curse.t: What the church itself has changed
dark-skin-curse.d: In 1981, "white and delightsome" became "pure and delightsome" at 2 Nephi 30:6. In 2010, racial wording came out of the chapter headings of 2 Nephi 5 and Mormon 5. In 2013 the Gospel Topics essay Race and the Priesthood disavowed the idea that dark skin marks God's disfavour.

Scripture Central, with the BYU scholars Ethan Sproat and Gerrit Steenblik, argue that "skin of blackness" may be a metaphor, or may mean garments and marks the Lamanites took on. On that reading the curse is separation from the Lord in 2 Nephi 5:20, and the mark is a separate thing. FAIR adds that the book itself condemns Nephite racism — Jacob 3:5-9 calls the Lamanites more righteous. In some episodes the two peoples cannot be told apart, which a stark skin difference would prevent. And the headings were 1981 study helps by Bruce R. McConkie, not scripture.

Strong for you, and this is one to make gently. The garment reading is recent. It cuts against nearly two centuries of the church's own teaching, from Brigham Young to Spencer W. Kimball, who reported Lamanite converts growing lighter. And the text's own chain resists it: cursed for iniquity, therefore a skin of blackness, so they would not be enticing.
"Read me 2 Nephi 5:21. What does it say the curse actually was?"

fortunate-fall.d: 2 Nephi 2:22-25 says Adam's fall was necessary and good. Without it, Adam and Eve "would have had no children." And "Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy." Alma 12:22-26 takes the same line.
Romans 5:12-19 treats the fall as sin. It brought death and condemnation, not joy. Romans 8:20-22 says creation was subjected to futility by it.

fortunate-fall.t: The verse that does the work
fortunate-fall.d: Genesis 1:28. God told Adam and Eve to "be fruitful, and multiply" before the fall. So the premise that there could be no children without the fall runs straight into that command.

And it is a real one. The BYU Religious Studies Center points to the felix culpa tradition — the happy fault. Ambrose taught it. Augustine wrote "O felix culpa." The Easter Exsultet sings it. Christians have long said God brings a greater good out of the fall. Scripture Central adds 2 Nephi 2:11: agency and joy need a world with opposition in it. And Eve is honoured here rather than blamed.

Genuinely arguable, and narrower than critics usually make it. Concede the felix culpa point at once. But notice the difference. That tradition celebrates redemption despite the fall. 2 Nephi 2 makes the fall itself necessary. Genesis 1:28 still has no strong published answer.
"God says be fruitful in Genesis 1:28. That's before the fall, isn't it?"

original-sin-infant-baptism.d: That little children "are not capable of committing sin." That infant baptism is "solemn mockery before God." And that anyone who thinks children need baptism "must go down to hell" if he dies in that thought. See Moroni 8:8-23.

original-sin-infant-baptism.t: What the Bible is usually quoted back
original-sin-infant-baptism.d: Psalm 51:5 says we are sinful from conception. Ephesians 2:3 calls us "by nature the children of wrath." Romans 5:12 and 18-19 say we are condemned in Adam.

FAIR makes three points, and they land. The Bible never commands infant baptism and never shows one. Baptists and most evangelicals end up where Moroni does. Second, the idea that we inherit Adam's guilt — and not just a fallen nature — comes from Augustine. The Eastern Orthodox reject it to this day. Third, Latter-day Saints teach that Christ covers Adam's fall for children, with no conditions. Moroni 8:8 says the curse of Adam is taken from them in him.

Not on infant baptism. Christians have argued that one among themselves for centuries. It stands on two narrower points. Moroni 8 sends almost every Christian before the Reformation to hell. No verse in the Bible allows that. And a record set in the fourth century is arguing a fight that belongs to Pelagius, to Augustine, and to revival preaching in the 1800s.
Do not use the simple version. If you argue Bible against Book of Mormon here, you will be arguing against a lot of Christians too. Use the narrow version or leave it.
"I don't baptise babies either. But why does Moroni send everyone who does to hell?"

no-semitic-inscriptions.d: A thousand years of continuous writing. Hebrew, and a modified Egyptian script, cut into metal plates and stone. See Mormon 9:32-34, 1 Nephi 1:2, Omni 1:20-22, Mosiah 8:11-13 and Jacob 4:1-3.

Nothing. No writing in Hebrew or Egyptian has ever been dug up in the Americas and proved real. Nor in any related script. No script called "reformed Egyptian" is known to Egyptologists. And the scripts we can read there — Maya, Zapotec, Epi-Olmec — are built on other lines. The signs are not the same.

Four objects come up. The Bat Creek Stone. The Los Lunas Decalogue Stone. The Newark Holy Stones. The Michigan Relics. Each one is a known fake, or is strongly suspected of being one. Do not lean on any of them.

Three lines. First, "reformed Egyptian" is the book's own phrase for a script "altered by us, according to our manner of speech." It is not a claim that Egyptologists should know the name. Egyptian really was reformed over time. It went from hieroglyphic to hieratic to demotic. And Hugh Nibley noted Semitic languages written in Egyptian letters. Second, this was a small record. A few men kept it on plates, and then it was buried. It was never public writing on walls. Third, Brian Stubbs works on Uto-Aztecan. He argues for about 1,500 matches with Semitic and Egyptian, and claims regular sound rules.

Strong for you. The small-record answer hangs together. But notice what it grants: there is now no way to test the claim. Stubbs is the one piece of evidence on the other side. No linguist outside the church has taken it up. Michael Coe, the Yale Maya scholar, said the field has found nothing.
"Has any inscription in the Americas ever been read as Hebrew or Egyptian?"

dna-native-american-origins.d: Three kinds of test have been run on Native American DNA. The mother line, called mitochondrial. The father line, from the Y chromosome. And the whole genome. All three point the same way: to Siberia and East Asia. People crossed at Beringia more than 15,000 years ago. No Middle Eastern founding line from about 600 BC has been found.

Two Latter-day Saint scientists. Thomas Murphy, an anthropologist, and Simon Southerton, a geneticist and former bishop. They published in 2002 and 2003. Murphy faced a disciplinary council, postponed 24 hours before it met. Southerton was disciplined.
The introduction to the Book of Mormon was quietly reworded. The Lamanites had been "the principal ancestors of the American Indians." They became "among the ancestors."

The church's own Gospel Topics essay grants that most Native Americans carry largely Asian DNA. Then it makes real points. The text never says Lehi's party was alone. A group of about 30 joining a large population leaves no detectable signal after 2,600 years. Founder effect, genetic drift and the bottleneck after contact each erase small lines. Ugo Perego notes the Asian ancestor of haplogroup X2a is itself missing from modern Asia. And the essay's own bottom line is that DNA "cannot be used decisively to either affirm or reject" the book.

Genuinely arguable, and be careful. The population genetics is sound, and anyone who says DNA disproves the book has overstated it. But look at the price. The answer works only by shrinking the Nephites into a small group inside a continent already full of Asians. 2 Nephi 1:8-9 says the land was "kept as yet from the knowledge of other nations." And it took an unannounced edit to the printed introduction.
"Why did the introduction change from 'principal ancestors' to 'among the ancestors'?"

population-growth-impossible.d: A founding party of about 20 to 30 lands around 589 BC. It splits almost at once. Within roughly 500 years the text reports 19,094 Lamanites killed in one battle at Alma 2:19. Later, 230,000 Nephites die at Cumorah in Mormon 6:10-15. The Jaredites reach "two millions" at Ether 15:2.

That reaching those figures from those founders needs growth rates far above anything measured in pre-modern populations. And the text has temples, kings and standing armies within two generations of a landing party of a couple of dozen.

This is one they answer well. James E. Smith is a professional historical demographer. He argues Kunich applied long-run averages to a frontier colony, where 2 to 3% a year is normal for centuries — colonial New England did it, and so did Pitcairn. His simulations produce Book of Mormon numbers. Polygamy is attested among Lamanites and early Nephites. Ancient casualty figures are notoriously inflated everywhere. And the book never says the land was empty: Sherem appears from nowhere in Jacob 7, and the Mulekites are found already numerous in Omni 1.

The fix and the DNA fix are the same fix. The more other people you put in the land, the less the book is what its own narrators thought it was. And the silence about a surrounding native majority becomes strange in itself.
Genuinely arguable, and weak on its own. Smith is right against Kunich on the demography. Use this one only alongside the DNA and archaeology cases, where it adds weight.
"If there were already people there, why does nobody in the book mention them?"

nephite-non-levite-priesthood.d: The Nephites kept the law of Moses strictly. See 2 Nephi 5:10 and 25:24. They offered burnt sacrifices too, at 1 Nephi 5:9 and Mosiah 2:3. Yet Nephi was of the tribe of Joseph, through Manasseh (Alma 10:3). And at 2 Nephi 5:26 he makes his brothers Jacob and Joseph priests.

The law of Moses restricted priesthood and sacrifice to Aaron's line inside Levi. See Numbers 3:9-12 and 16:39-40. Hebrews 7:13-14 says plainly that of another tribe "no man gave attendance at the altar." 2 Chronicles 26:16-21 shows what happened when a king tried.

That the Nephites held the higher Melchizedek priesthood. Jacob was ordained "after the manner of his holy order" at 2 Nephi 6:2, and Alma 13 develops it. That order predates Levi in the Bible itself — Genesis 14, Psalm 110, Hebrews 7:4-10. They add three things. The book never claims Levitical authority. No Levites came with Lehi. And real Jewish communities of that era ran altars outside Jerusalem, at Elephantine and Arad.

Genuinely arguable, and this is a small case. Alma 13 gives them a textual base, and Elephantine is real history. The tension is that Hebrews 7 treats a non-Levitical priesthood as incompatible with the law the Nephites claim to keep in all things.
"How does a man from Joseph's tribe offer sacrifice under Moses' law?"

temples-outside-jerusalem.d: Nephi builds a temple "after the manner of the temple of Solomon" at 2 Nephi 5:16. Later there are temples in several cities — Alma 16:13, Alma 26:29, Helaman 3:9 and 3:14.

Deuteronomy 12:5-14 confines sacrifice to "the place which the LORD your God shall choose." After Solomon that meant Jerusalem alone, as 1 Kings 8:29 assumes. And Josiah's reform, within living memory of Lehi leaving, had destroyed the rival sanctuaries — 2 Kings 23:4-20.

FAIR points to real Jewish temples outside Jerusalem. The sacrificial temple at Elephantine in Egypt. The sanctuary at Arad. Leontopolis later. So Jews far from Jerusalem did build temples. FAIR argues the centralisation command applied inside the land of Israel, not to a colony cut off across an ocean.

Genuinely arguable, and this is a minor one. Elephantine and Arad are archaeological facts and they blunt the word unthinkable. The remaining point is narrow. Those sites are judged irregular against the law. The Book of Mormon presents its temples as fully legitimate.
"Deuteronomy 12 says one place. How did Nephi read that?"

christ-remains-in-heaven-acts-3.d: 3 Nephi 11-28 has the risen Christ come down and minister to the Nephites in the body for days. Against that, Acts 3:20-21 calls Jesus one "whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things." So, the argument goes, he cannot have been in America.

The New Testament records him appearing after the ascension more than once. To Stephen in Acts 7:55-56. To Paul on the Damascus road in Acts 9:3-6 and 1 Corinthians 15:8. To John on Patmos in Revelation 1:12-18.

christ-remains-in-heaven-acts-3.t: So what does the verse mean
christ-remains-in-heaven-acts-3.d: Where Christ resides between the ascension and the last day. It is not a rule against him appearing. Their reply is simply correct here.
FAIR gives exactly those three appearances and says the Nephite visit is the same kind of thing on a larger scale. They also read "other sheep I have" in John 10:16 as Jesus anticipating it.
Do not use this one. There are real problems with 3 Nephi and they are covered elsewhere. Acts 3:21 is not one of them, and using it will cost you your credibility on the cases that do work.
Nothing. If someone else raises it, say plainly that you don't think it holds.

joseph-smith-failed-prophecies.d: D&C 84:2-5, given in September 1832. A temple "shall be reared in this generation" on the dedicated lot at Independence, Missouri. And "verily this generation shall not all pass away until an house shall be built unto the Lord."

No temple was ever built there. Every member of that generation is long dead. Two related cases sit beside it. D&C 114:1 called David W. Patten on a mission "next spring"; he was killed months before it. And there is the 1835 statement about the Second Coming in fifty-six years.
Deuteronomy 18:20-22. A prophet whose word "follow not, nor come to pass" has spoken presumptuously. Jeremiah 28:9 and Ezekiel 33:33 are used the same way.

FAIR says biblical prophecy is often conditional without saying so. Jonah announced flatly that in forty days Nineveh would be overthrown. It was not, and Jonah was no false prophet. And D&C 124:49-51, from 1841, canonises that principle: when enemies stop a commanded work, God "requires that work no more." The Saints were driven out of Jackson County in 1833. Others read "an house" as the Kirtland temple of 1836.

Genuinely arguable. The non-fulfilment is not in dispute, and the wording reads like a dated, unconditional oracle — Orson Pratt kept reaffirming it as one. But the Jonah precedent is real, and the conditionality clause is inside their own canon. This turns on how you read prophecy, not on a disputed fact.
"How do you tell a conditional prophecy from one that just failed?"

exaltation-eternal-progression.d: D&C 132:19-20 says the faithful sealed in celestial marriage "shall pass by the angels, and the gods." Then "shall they be gods, because they have no end… because they have all power." Joseph Smith's King Follett sermon of 1844 taught that God "was once a man like us," and that the Saints must learn "how to be gods yourselves." Lorenzo Snow put it in a couplet: as man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may be.

The 2014 essay Becoming Like God complains that this gets reduced to a cartoon about people getting their own planets. Fair enough. But read on. The essay reaffirms the substance — exaltation to godhood, with the power to create.

Isaiah 43:10 has God say "before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me." Isaiah 44:6-8 and 45:5 say the same. And notice who first offered godhood in Scripture. The serpent, in Genesis 3:5: "ye shall be as gods."

And it is serious. Deification language runs through early Christianity. Psalm 82:6, quoted by Jesus in John 10:34: "Ye are gods." 2 Peter 1:4 on being "partakers of the divine nature." Romans 8:17 on being joint-heirs with Christ. Irenaeus taught it, and Clement of Alexandria wrote that the Word became man so that man might learn how to become God. On this reading the church restores theosis, not polytheism. Isaiah's denials are aimed at idols. And exalted beings stay forever subordinate to the Father.

Strong for you, but you must handle theosis honestly or you will lose. Early Christian deification always kept the line between Creator and creature. It never taught that God was once a man, and never made the deified gods in the sense D&C 132 describes. Isaiah 43:10 is about existence, and it is still standing.
"Isaiah 43:10 says no God will be formed after him. How do you read that?"

heavenly-mother-doctrine.d: The 2015 essay Mother in Heaven calls it "cherished and distinctive" doctrine that every human spirit is the child of a Heavenly Father and a Heavenly Mother. It rests on Joseph Smith's teaching of a pre-mortal spirit life — Abraham 3:22-26 and D&C 93:29 — and was carried by Eliza R. Snow's hymn O My Father.

Two things, in its own words. That present knowledge about a Mother in Heaven "is limited." And that "there is no record of a formal revelation to Joseph Smith on this doctrine." It also directs members not to pray to her.

Nothing. The only "queen of heaven" in it is an idolatrous cult that Jeremiah condemns, at Jeremiah 7:18 and 44:17-25. Deuteronomy 6:4 says the LORD is one. Isaiah 44:6-8 says there is no God beside him.

The essay, with a survey of some 600 historical references by David Paulsen and Martin Pulido, presents her as a reasoned consequence of restored truth. If humans are literally God's spirit children, made male and female in the divine image at Genesis 1:26-27, then eternal parenthood implies a Mother. And silence in the Bible is not denial, because Latter-day Saints do not treat the Bible as complete. Worship still goes to the Father alone, in Christ's name.

Strong for you, and gently made. The church concedes the two facts that matter: no biblical text, and no recorded revelation. The corollary argument is coherent inside their own premises. It supplies no scripture, and scripture is the thing at issue.
"The essay says there was no formal revelation on this. Where does it come from?"

jesus-firstborn-spirit-attained-godhood.d: That Jesus is the firstborn spirit child of Heavenly Father and heavenly parents. Gospel Principles, chapters 2 and 3, says so. That makes him the literal elder brother of every human, of the same kind as us. James Talmage's Jesus the Christ says he "attained the rank of Godhood" before this life.

John 1:3 — "All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made." That scope leaves Christ outside the category of made things. Colossians 1:17 says "he is before all things." Micah 5:2 says his goings forth are "from everlasting." Hebrews 13:8 says he is the same yesterday, today and forever. John 8:58 has him say "before Abraham was, I am."

He did not become divine late. He is Jehovah, the God of the Old Testament — The Living Christ, 2000, says so directly. D&C 93:21 calls him the Firstborn who was in the beginning with the Father, and Moses 1:33 has him creating worlds without number. On Colossians 1:15 they note Paul himself calls Christ "the firstborn of every creature." And FAIR argues the Greek at Colossians 1:16 means organising existing material, not making something from nothing.

Colossians 1:16 explains its own firstborn line: "for by him were all things created." He is first over creation because he made it. And the deeper problem is not a proof text. Even granting that Christ was Jehovah before the world, this makes him a begotten spirit sibling whose divinity was attained. That is a different kind of being from the eternal Creator who came down.
Strong for you. But say the strong half of their case first — the Jehovah identification is real and most Christians do not know they teach it. Then ask about John 1:3.
"Was there ever a time when Jesus was not God?"

js-polygamy-wives-count-ages.d: Joseph Smith was sealed to roughly 30 to 40 women. That number is not a critic's. The Gospel Topics essay says "careful estimates put the number between 30 and 40."
Helen Mar Kimball, sealed "several months before her 15th birthday." She was 14. And Fanny Alger, about 16, a servant in the Smith home.

In a letter dated 21 January 1838 he called the Alger matter "a dirty, nasty, filthy scrape." Cowdery was one of the Three Witnesses. He was cut off from the church soon after. The charge was falsely insinuating that Smith was guilty of adultery.

The church grants the marriages. It frames them as a commanded restoration of Old Testament plural marriage, which Smith resisted. Brian Hales argues Helen's sealing was likely "eternity only" and dynastic — a link between the Kimball and Smith families, with no evidence of a marital relationship. She went on living with her parents. Marriage at 14 to 16 was legal, and not unheard of on the frontier in the 1840s. And on later accounts Fanny Alger was a marriage with her parents' consent, not an affair.

They admit this themselves. The count, the 14-year-old and the secrecy are all in the church's own essay. Their answers go to what it meant, not to whether it happened. Eternity-only is possible and cannot be proved. And frontier custom does not explain why it was kept from Emma and from the church.
"The church's own essay says thirty to forty. Have you read it?"

js-polyandry.d: Being sealed to a woman who already had a living husband.

Roughly 11 of Joseph Smith's plural wives were civilly married to living husbands at the time. Todd Compton puts that at about a third of them. The church's own essay concedes he was sealed to "a number of women who were already married."

Zina Diantha Huntington. She was sealed to Smith in October 1841, about seven months after she married Henry Jacobs. Smith had told her that an angel with a drawn sword threatened his position and his life if plural marriage was not established. She went on living with Jacobs.

Brian Hales argues most of these were "eternity only" — a link for the next life that left the earthly marriage alone. That is why husbands like Henry Jacobs stayed in the home, and some stayed faithful members. There is hard evidence too. In 2016 Ugo Perego's DNA testing ruled Smith out as the father of Josephine Lyon. Her mother was the polyandrous wife with the strongest documentary claim of a marital relationship. No verified child of Smith by any plural wife has ever been identified. And the essay itself allows that these sealings may have been about eternal linking.

They admit the sealings. Whether there were sexual relations is genuinely contested, and the DNA result is a real win for them. Do not claim proven sexual polyandry. You cannot support it. What stands on primary sources is the sealing itself — to other men's wives, under angelic threat, and in secret.
"Were any of the women he was sealed to already married?"

dc132-emma-destroyed.d: D&C 132, dictated on 12 July 1843. It is still canonised scripture. You can read it in any current Doctrine and Covenants.

It names her. Verse 52 commands her to "receive all those that have been given unto my servant Joseph." Verse 54 warns that "if she will not abide this commandment she shall be destroyed, saith the Lord." Verse 64 extends that to any first wife who refuses consent.
It was dictated after Smith had already married most of his plural wives. Emma did not know, and had not consented.

That "destroyed" is covenant language, not physical death — losing the blessings of the covenant, as in verse 26. And no harm came to Emma. She refused, burned her copy, and stayed his wife. The section is framed as an Abrahamic test, and it promises her blessings for obedience too. Richard Bushman notes it was written down at Hyrum's request, precisely to persuade her. That is a family crisis, not a death threat.

They admit the text, and nobody disputes it. The softer reading of "destroyed" is plausible. It does not change what the verse does. Canonised scripture makes a named woman's standing depend on accepting her husband's other wives. Read Ephesians 5:25 beside it and let it sit.
"Can we read D&C 132:52-54 together? I'd like to know how you hear it."

js-polygamy-denials.d: On 26 May 1844, a month before he died, Joseph Smith preached this. "What a thing it is for a man to be accused of committing adultery, and having seven wives, when I can only find one." It is in History of the Church 6:411.
He had been sealed to more than thirty women.

The 1835 Article on Marriage declared one man and one wife. It stayed in the Doctrine and Covenants until 1876. Church papers denied "spiritual wifery" right through the Nauvoo years, while the practice spread quietly among the leaders.

FAIR says the denials were carefully worded. He denied adultery. He denied John C. Bennett's freelance "spiritual wifery." He did not deny celestial marriage given by God. He had one legal wife, so "I can only find one" was technically true. Telling the truth openly would have brought mobs and prosecution, as the Expositor affair proved. Concealment protected the community. Apologists compare Abraham's misdirection about Sarah. And the church's own essay grants the secrecy, and says those involved found it agonising.

They admit the facts and defend them as justified. That is the whole argument. But a carefully worded statement meant to leave a false impression is still deception. Proverbs 12:22 and Ephesians 4:25 are the measures, and that is what is being weighed here.
"He said he could only find one wife. How many was he sealed to that month?"

eternal-polygamy-today.d: A widowed man may be sealed to a second wife while he is still sealed to the first. Two church presidents are in that position. Russell M. Nelson was sealed to Wendy Watson in 2006, after Dantzel died. Dallin H. Oaks was sealed to Kristen McMain in 2000, after June died. Each is sealed to two women for eternity.

eternal-polygamy-today.t: The part that is not equal
eternal-polygamy-today.d: A living woman cannot be sealed to a second man unless the first sealing is cancelled. And D&C 132 has never been removed from the canon.

Carol Lynn Pearson gathered the accounts in The Ghost of Eternal Polygamy, published in 2016. They are believing Latter-day Saint women who expect to be shared in eternity. This is grief, not a debating point.

Dallin H. Oaks answered it directly in General Conference in October 2019. The church makes no doctrinal claim about how families are arranged in the next life. Trust the Lord. Sealing tangles will be sorted out by a loving God, and nobody will be given an eternal arrangement they do not want. Since 1998, deceased women may be sealed by proxy to every man they married in life, on the assumption that she will choose. The rule about living women is administrative. And the church has not practised plural marriage since 1904; it excommunicates those who do.

They admit the policy. It is in the Handbook and it is public. Oaks's answer is a candid "we don't know," and that is worth respecting. It also settles nothing. The gap between what a widower may do and what a widow may do is still in force.
"If a man's wife dies he can be sealed again. Can a woman?"

polygamy-coercion-angel-sword.d: The essay Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo states that Joseph Smith told women an angel appeared three times commanding polygamy. On the last visit "the angel came with a drawn sword, threatening Joseph with destruction unless he went forward."

In proposals. To Zina Diantha Huntington, while she was courting Henry Jacobs. She was sealed to Joseph after being told of the angel, and Henry later stood as a witness. To Mary Elizabeth Rollins Lightner, who was already married. And to Lucy Walker, who was 16 and living in his home after her mother died. She was told to seek her own confirmation. She later wrote about her anguish.

She was 14. She wrote down what Joseph promised her: "If you will take this step, it will ensure your eternal salvation and exaltation, and that of your father's household." That is her own memoir, written as a faithful member of the church.

Brian Hales and FAIR say the angel accounts come from faithful participants, and that they show reluctance rather than appetite. He delayed for years, and moved only under compulsion from God. Helen's sealing was likely unconsummated and dynastic, linking families for the next life. Women did refuse — Sarah Pratt and Cordelia Morley both did, with no spiritual penalty. And marriage customs for young women in the 1840s were not ours.

They admit the facts. Look at what the answer itself says. An angel threatened him into it. So a proposal carried a promise from God and a threat from God at the same time. D&C 132:54 and 64 put the threat into scripture. Galatians 1:8 speaks to exactly this, and 2 Corinthians 11:14 warns that Satan appears as an angel of light.
"Helen was fourteen. What do you make of what she was promised?"

post-manifesto-polygamy.d: The 1890 Manifesto, now Official Declaration 1, publicly ended plural marriage. Leaders then repeatedly denied that any new plural marriages were taking place.

Apostles and members of the First Presidency secretly authorised or performed roughly 250 new plural marriages between 1890 and 1904. That is D. Michael Quinn's count, published in Dialogue in 1985. B. Carmon Hardy documents 262 in Solemn Covenant. Many took place in Mexico, in Canada, or at sea. Nine or ten General Authorities took new plural wives themselves.

The Reed Smoot Senate hearings, from 1904 to 1907. In March 1904 the church president Joseph F. Smith testified under oath. He had gone on living with his five plural wives, and had fathered eleven children by them since 1890, against the law. Weeks later he issued the Second Manifesto. Apostles John W. Taylor and Matthias F. Cowley were forced out of the Quorum of the Twelve.

The church's own essay concedes most of it. Marriages "continued to be quietly performed" in Mexico and Canada. The Manifesto was about the laws of the United States, and "said nothing about the laws of other nations," so leaders read it as limited. Many believed it only suspended the practice for a time. Existing husbands kept their covenant families rather than abandon them. Only in 1904 were members "put on notice." The transition away from something leaders believed God had commanded was wrenching, and it happened under federal persecution.

They admit almost all of it, in their own essay. Joseph F. Smith's sworn testimony is a church president admitting it himself. What is argued is motive — sincere confusion rather than duplicity. But the Second Manifesto said no marriages had happened with the "sanction, consent or knowledge of the Church," and Quinn and Hardy document that they had. And this is the second time, after Nauvoo.
"What did Joseph F. Smith tell the Senate in 1904?"

avoid-87-wives-overclaim.d: That Joseph Smith had 87 wives. Or 50. Or hundreds.

The documented count is about 30 to 40. Todd Compton documents 33. The higher figures — Stanley Ivins once tallied 84 — pad the list with sealings nobody can verify, and with sealings performed after his death.
Say 87 and your friend corrects your arithmetic. Then they walk away from everything else you were going to say. You handed them the exit.

Their own number. The Gospel Topics essay says "careful estimates put the number between 30 and 40," citing Brian Hales. Add a bride aged 14, about a dozen women with living husbands, and years of public denials. Every clause of that is footnoted to the church's own website.
Do not use it. Overclaiming is the one gift you can hand FAIR on this subject. The admitted facts need no help from you.
"Thirty to forty. That's your church's number, on your church's website."

avoid-mainstream-polygamy-today.d: That Mormons still practise polygamy. Usually with prairie dresses and plural households in mind.

Since the 1904 Second Manifesto, contracting or performing a plural marriage means excommunication. The people in those pictures are FLDS, or AUB, or independents. They are splinter groups, and the church denounces them.
Confusing the Latter-day Saints with the FLDS is the fastest way to be politely dismissed. And you will have earned it.

Drop the claim about living people and the doctrinal one is untouched. D&C 132 is still canonised scripture. Widowed men are sealed for eternity to more than one wife today; Presidents Nelson and Oaks both are. And the church's own history has leaders secretly authorising plural marriages for fourteen years after 1890.
Do not use it as stated. Concede it fully and quickly, then ask the doctrinal question. That is worth far more than the point you gave up.
"You're right, nobody practises it now. So why is the revelation still in your scriptures?"

priesthood-temple-ban-1852-1978.d: From Brigham Young's announcements in 1852 until June 1978, the church barred members of Black African descent. Men could not be ordained to the priesthood. Men and women could not receive the temple endowment or be sealed. In the church's own teaching, those are the ordinances required for exaltation. It lasted 126 years.

priesthood-temple-ban-1852-1978.t: How it was defended at the time
priesthood-temple-ban-1852-1978.d: First Presidency statements in 1949 and again in 1969 called it divinely instituted. They grounded it in conduct before this life, and in the curse of Cain.

The 2013 Gospel Topics essay Race and the Priesthood disavows "the theories advanced in the past." It places the ban's origin in the racial culture of 1850s America. And it says there was no founding revelation.

It leans on that essay, and it is honest work. Joseph Smith ordained Black men — Elijah Able and Q. Walker Lewis. The restriction began under Young, without a recorded revelation. It was ended by revelation to Spencer W. Kimball in 1978. Every theological justification has been repudiated. Apologists add a parallel from Acts: the gospel was withheld from Gentiles until Peter's vision. God lifts restrictions on his own timetable, through living prophets. And a church willing to disavow its leaders' errors is showing revelation at work, not disproving it.

The Acts parallel cuts the other way. Peter's revelation ended ethnic exclusion at the very start of the church. Here the ban was brought in after an inclusive start. Prophets then defended it as doctrine for over a century. And its reasons are now officially disavowed. Real people carried that for six generations. The question about prophetic reliability is still there.
"Acts 10:34 says God is no respecter of persons. How do you hold that with 1852 to 1978?"

mountain-meadows-massacre.d: On 11 September 1857, Mormon militiamen of the Iron County brigade lured the Baker-Fancher wagon train out under a white flag. The emigrants had already surrendered. About 120 men, women and children were murdered. Only the small children were spared.

Local church and militia leaders in the Cedar City area. Among them the stake president Isaac Haight, and Bishop John D. Lee. Lee was the only person ever executed for it, twenty years later, in 1877.

The church's own sponsored history. Massacre at Mountain Meadows, by Ronald Walker, Richard Turley and Glen Leonard, published by Oxford in 2008. It confirms that local church leaders were responsible. In 2007 Elder Henry B. Eyring expressed "profound regret" for the First Presidency.

The church acknowledges the massacre and its horror in full. The context was the Utah War. A federal army was approaching. Memories of Missouri and Nauvoo were fresh, and the preaching of the moment was inflamed. The church's own history concludes that Brigham Young did not order it; his letter counselling that the train be allowed to pass arrived two days late. Local leaders acted against that counsel. Participants were later excommunicated. The church has built memorials, worked with descendants, and published the fullest account itself.

They admit this themselves, and every serious party agrees on the facts. Do not say Brigham Young ordered it. The documentary evidence does not support that, and their own historians say otherwise. What is conceded is heavy enough. Church leaders at the Cedar City level planned the mass murder of unarmed families.
"Have you read the church's own book on Mountain Meadows? It doesn't spare anyone."

blood-atonement.d: That some sins go beyond what Christ's blood can reach, and need the sinner's own. From the Tabernacle pulpit in 1856 he said that such men, if their eyes were open, "would be perfectly willing to have their blood spilt upon the ground, that the smoke thereof might ascend to heaven as an offering for their sins." It is in the Journal of Discourses 4:53-54, and again at 4:219-220 in 1857.

Hebrews 10:14 — "by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified." 1 John 1:7 — the blood of Jesus Christ "cleanseth us from all sin." And John 19:30 — "It is finished." See also Hebrews 9:26 and 1 Timothy 2:5-6.
In June 2010 it stated formally that "so-called blood atonement… is not a doctrine of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints." Bruce R. McConkie had repudiated it in a letter in 1978.

FAIR and Mormonr make four points. The language belongs to the heated preaching of the Mormon Reformation in 1856 and 1857, and was meant to provoke repentance. It was framed as voluntary, and tied to capital punishment for capital crimes, echoing Genesis 9:6 — not to vigilante killing. It was never canonised; D&C 42:18 and 42:79 prescribe excommunication and the civil courts. And the church has repudiated it by name.

Strong for you, and use it gently. Both the sermons and the disavowal are documented. What Young preached — that some sins lie beyond the reach of Christ's blood — flatly contradicts Hebrews 10:14 and 1 John 1:7. The hyperbole reading strains against his own words, which are sober counsel across several sermons and years. The weight of this now is not the doctrine. It is that a prophet taught from the pulpit what the church now calls false.
"Is there any sin Christ's blood cannot reach? Hebrews 10:14 says no."

abuse-helpline-2022.d: In 2022 the Associated Press published an investigation drawing on about 12,000 pages of sealed records. It reported that the church's abuse help line routes a bishop's report of child sexual abuse to church lawyers, the firm Kirton McConkie, rather than to police.

Paul Adams confessed to two bishops, beginning in 2011, that he was abusing his daughter. Church counsel advised that Arizona's clergy-penitent privilege barred reporting. The abuse went on for about seven more years. It came to include a second daughter, an infant. Adams was caught independently in 2017.

The church calls the AP framing egregiously wrong, and its case is not weak. The bishop repeatedly urged Adams and his wife to report it, and tried to intervene. Arizona law made the confession privileged. He could not legally pass on what he learned in it without consent. Arizona's courts agreed. In 2023 the state supreme court upheld the privilege and dismissed the claims. The help line exists so that untrained lay bishops reach professionals at once. Those professionals tell them how to comply with reporting law, which differs in every state. Others knew too — the mother, and people who saw what Adams posted online — and they did not report either.

Genuinely arguable, and this one needs care. The timeline is not disputed: a confession in 2011, no report, and seven more years. A child was harmed in that gap. What is contested is why. The legal advice tracked the actual Arizona statute, and the courts sided with the church. What no answer removes is that the system produced this outcome, and that these calls run through defence counsel.
"When a bishop calls that line, who is on the other end?"

oath-of-vengeance.d: From about 1845 until about 1927, the temple endowment included a covenant. It bound the member to "pray and never cease to pray Almighty God to avenge the blood of the prophets upon this nation," and to teach the same to children and grandchildren, to the third and fourth generation.
It was documented under oath. The Reed Smoot hearings in the United States Senate, from 1904 to 1906, put it on the record. No informed apologist denies that it existed.
It was quietly removed around 1927, during the church's assimilation era. There was no public explanation and no repudiation.

FAIR points out that the oath asked God to avenge. It did not commit anyone to take vengeance themselves. That is close to the martyrs' cry in Revelation 6:10 — "How long, O Lord… dost thou not judge and avenge our blood?" — and to the imprecatory Psalms. It arose in the raw aftermath of the murders of Joseph and Hyrum Smith, for which nobody was ever convicted. It was removed as the wound healed. And temple ceremonies have always been revised.
