Strong for you, and the Revelation 6:10 point is fair — take the caricature off the table first. What stands is the documented thing. A prayer for vengeance on a nation, to be handed down for four generations, inside the faith's holiest ordinance. Set that beside Matthew 5:44, where Jesus tells us to pray for our enemies.
"Jesus says pray for those who persecute you. How does that sit with the old covenant?"

danites-1838.d: A secret armed band of Mormons in Missouri, in 1838. Sampson Avard set it up. They bullied church dissenters and drove them out. The Danite Manifesto named names. It threatened Oliver Cowdery, the Whitmers and others.
In the fighting of October 1838, Mormon forces raided and burned two towns that were not Mormon. Gallatin and Millport. Danites rode with them.

How much Joseph Smith knew, and how much he told them to do. Avard testified that Smith was the mastermind. Stephen LeSueur argues that Smith backed the Danites and gained by them. Scholars close to the church argue that Avard ran his own show.

Avard was a self-serving opportunist who turned state's witness to save himself, and was excommunicated in 1839. That makes his testimony the least reliable kind. Leland Gentry and Alexander Baugh trace three phases: a legitimate community defence that Avard corrupted into secret oaths and plunder, without Smith's authorisation. And the context was existential. Mormons were being burned out. Governor Boggs's Extermination Order and the Haun's Mill massacre followed within weeks. Mormon violence was real, and it was a fraction of what was done to them.

Genuinely arguable, and honest historians divide here. The Danites, the expulsions and the raids are not disputed. Smith's personal authorisation rests largely on Avard's compromised word. Smith praised Danite leaders publicly and rode the wave. Operational command is not established.
"How much do you think Joseph knew about the Danites? Historians don't agree either."

nauvoo-expositor-carthage.d: Joseph Smith was mayor of Nauvoo. He and the city council ordered the press of the Nauvoo Expositor destroyed. The paper had printed one issue, on 7 June. It reported his secret plural marriage. It reported his teaching that there is more than one god. On both counts it was telling the truth.
Riot charges. Smith's surrender at Carthage. And the mob attack of 27 June in which he and Hyrum were killed.

nauvoo-expositor-carthage.t: The detail devotional accounts leave out
nauvoo-expositor-carthage.d: At Carthage, Smith fired a smuggled six-shot pepperbox pistol into the mob. He wounded three men. That is John Taylor's own account, in History of the Church 7:102-103. Devotional retellings left it out for a long time.

Dallin H. Oaks published a legal analysis in the Utah Law Review in 1965. Before the Fourteenth Amendment, the First Amendment did not bind city governments. So abating a newspaper as a nuisance had some legal footing under the Nauvoo Charter. Oaks concedes that destroying the press itself probably went beyond that. The council feared the paper would bring a mob — and it did. On Carthage: defending yourself against a lynch mob does not make the killing just. Smith was in state custody under the governor's pledged protection. The pistol is recorded by an eyewitness, and the church has published the fact in Saints.

They admit the facts, and so should you. Both things are true at once. The killing at Carthage was extrajudicial murder. And the trigger for it was the suppression of a newspaper that was telling the truth. Do not use the pistol to sneer; use it to ask what the word martyr is doing.

policy-of-exclusion-2015.d: The church Handbook was changed. Members in same-sex marriages were labelled apostates, subject to mandatory discipline. Their children could not receive a baby blessing or be baptised until they were 18. Baptism was then conditioned on disavowing their parents' marriage and leaving home.
In January 2016, President Russell M. Nelson publicly declared the policy a revelation. It was, he said, "the mind of the Lord and the will of the Lord," revealed to President Monson.
The church reversed both provisions. The reversal was also framed as directed by the Lord. Four years, and families carried the cost in between.

That both the policy and the reversal were inspired responses to circumstances, not eternal doctrine in conflict. The 2015 policy was meant to protect children from being caught between home and church — the same reasoning already applied to children of polygamists. By 2019, leaders concluded through continuing revelation that it did more harm than it prevented. Continuing revelation allows course correction; Acts 10, where the exclusion of Gentiles is reversed, is the template apologists cite. Policies implement doctrine for a time and a place, and the underlying doctrine of marriage never changed.

They admit every fact, including Nelson's own "will of the Lord" wording — which closes off the easier defence that it was only ever policy. The continuing-revelation argument is coherent on its own terms. It concedes the sequence rather than refuting it. Deuteronomy 24:16 and Ezekiel 18:20 say a child does not bear the parent's guilt.
"It was called the will of the Lord in 2016 and reversed in 2019. How do you read that?"

quitmormon-resignation-difficulty.d: You write to your bishop. The request goes on to the stake president. There are waiting periods. Leaders reach out to you. Many people who resign say the visits and calls went on. They went on even after they had asked to be left alone.

A Utah attorney named Mark Naugle set up a free service, QuitMormon.com. It sends the resignation as legal representation. The church then deals with a lawyer, not with the member. Since 2015 it has processed on the order of 150,000 resignations.
The church added a notarisation requirement for QuitMormon submissions. It cited fraudulent requests. That added a step, and friction, to resigning through a third party.

The General Handbook already sets out a free official path. A member writes to the bishop and asks that the record be removed. The request is to be honoured. Leaders are told to check who the person is. They are told to make sure the person knows what follows. The church says those steps guard against fake or rushed removals. It says the 2019 rule came after real fake requests. Some were pranks that resigned other people. Follow-up contact is care from lay leaders, who are taught to answer with love. And any member may simply stop coming, with no penalty at all.

Strong for you, and keep it factual. The scale of QuitMormon has been reported in the mainstream press. Both sides confirm the 2019 rule. And the reports of contact after leaving are many. A legal buffer is the whole point of the service. What is argued here is motive, not fact.
"If leaving is simple, why do a hundred and fifty thousand people need a lawyer to do it?"

temple-wedding-family-exclusion.d: Only members with a current temple recommend may attend a sealing. So a parent who is not a member, or has resigned, or does not hold a recommend, waits outside while their child is married.

In the United States, a couple could hold a civil ceremony first, so that the excluded family could be there. If they did, they then had to wait a year to be sealed. That pushed couples to choose the temple over the people who could not come in.
The First Presidency removed the one-year wait in May 2019. Their letter gave the reason plainly: families were feeling excluded. The recommend rule for attending a sealing is unchanged.

That the temple is a sacred place, and its ordinances ask for covenant worthiness. The same bar applies to everyone, for every temple rite. It is not aimed at wedding guests. And the 2019 letter says its own reason: "when a temple marriage would cause parents or immediate family members to feel excluded, a civil marriage followed by a temple sealing is authorized." So a couple may now hold a wedding that no one is shut out of, and be sealed right after.

They admit this themselves. The rule and the old one-year penalty are documented church policy. The 2019 letter names the harm it was fixing. That change is a real improvement, and you should say so. It also confirms the underlying facts rather than answering them.
"Would your parents be able to come in?"

byu-honor-code-disaffiliation.d: BYU asks every student for a yearly sign-off from a church leader. It calls that an ecclesiastical endorsement. BYU's own written policy says the sign-off is pulled at once if a student is cut off from the church, put under formal discipline, or simply resigns.
Good standing under the Honor Code. The right to stay enrolled. A job on campus. A room on campus. And the degree itself, even if all the course work is done.

A student who stops believing halfway through a degree faces being thrown out. Or years of hiding it. A student who was never a member may attend, at a higher fee. So a member who leaves is treated worse than someone never baptised. FreeBYU took the matter to the accrediting bodies and lost. A narrow appeal route was added in 2015 and 2016.

BYU is a private religious school, paid for in large part by tithing. Latter-day Saint students pay a much lower fee, and the faith community makes up the rest. The deal is stated up front. Stay in good standing with the church that funds you. Students agree to that when they enrol. BYU notes that the accrediting bodies and the American Bar Association have upheld its right to set religious terms. An appeal route now exists for a student who resigns. And every student needs the yearly sign-off, member or not.

They admit this themselves; the rule is in BYU's own papers. So do not argue about the facts. The real question is what to call it. A private school setting religious terms, or a penalty for changing your mind. Ask it as a question, not as a charge.
"What happens to a BYU student who stops believing in their third year?"

social-costs-shunning.d: Strain in a marriage. Being cut off by family. Losing the community. Being pushed to the edge of a world that was everything. NPR and HuffPost have reported these patterns, and thousands of first-hand accounts say the same.

Part of it is teaching. A family split by faith loses the hope of being sealed for ever. And the word apostate carries real weight. Boyd K. Packer's 1993 talk named "so-called scholars," feminists and gays as dangers, and that shaped the mood.

There is no formal shunning here. Unlike the Jehovah's Witnesses, this church has no rule that tells a member to cut anyone off. No teaching, no handbook line, no discipline. Say that plainly, because it is true.

Church leaders have spoken against it, more than once and by name. Elder D. Todd Christofferson said in public that he "would not cut that child out of family life." Official teaching tells members to keep loving family who go. And broken ties follow a change of faith in many traditions. That is how families behave, not what the church asks.

Genuinely arguable, and both halves are true at once. The harm is well attested. So is the lack of any order to shun. What is argued is whether the church drives it. The written rule tells people not to pull away. The teaching and the mood can still reward it.
"What would change at home if you stopped going?"

grenfell-exit-testimony.d: Alyssa Grenfell. A BYU graduate, now an ex-Mormon writer with a YouTube channel of about 570,000 subscribers. Her book is How to Leave the Mormon Church: An Exmormon's Guide to Rebuilding After Religion, from 2023.

Three things. That ward representatives keep contacting and visiting after a member has stepped away. That wearing the garment every day works as a kind of bodily check, so stopping is a visible and costly signal. And that deconstruction costs you identity, family and friends.

grenfell-exit-testimony.t: How much of it is checkable
grenfell-exit-testimony.d: The pattern is. Continued contact after leaving matches what the resignation and QuitMormon cases document. Garment expectations are set out in the church's own General Handbook, at 38.5. Specific incidents in a memoir are one person's testimony, and should be labelled that way.

The church does not reply to individual memoirs. Its standing position is that members who step away are still loved and welcome. Ministering visits are voluntary pastoral care, and they stop when a person asks or resigns. The garment is a sacred private covenant freely taken in the temple, not surveillance. Apologists would add that a monetised ex-Mormon media career has its own incentives, and that one story should not stand for a church of 17 million.

Genuinely arguable, and use it carefully. Her core claims are corroborated at the level of pattern, by church policy documents and independent reporting. The individual incidents are not independently verified. Treat her as a representative voice, not as proof.
"Have you heard how people describe the first year after leaving?"

ces-letter-gospel-topics-visibility.d: In 2013 Jeremy Runnells compiled a list of historical problems and sent it to a director in the Church Educational System. He never got an answer. The document became the most widely circulated exit letter in modern Mormonism. Runnells was summoned to a disciplinary council and resigned in 2016.

ces-letter-gospel-topics-visibility.t: What the church published at the same time
ces-letter-gospel-topics-visibility.d: Thirteen Gospel Topics Essays, between 2013 and 2015. They concede facts that had long been denied. Multiple First Vision accounts. Translation by seer stone. Joseph Smith's polygamy.

With no announcement. Unsigned. Buried in the topics database of the website. Elder Steven E. Snow, then Church Historian, acknowledged the deliberate "soft roll out." In some wards, members who taught from the essays were rebuked by local leaders.

The church did the thing critics had asked for. It published frank, scholar-checked essays on its hardest topics, on its own site, and later folded that history into the Saints volumes and the curriculum. Snow's explanation of the quiet release was pastoral rather than secretive. Most members were not troubled by these issues, and the essays were placed where a searching member would find them. FAIR argues the CES Letter is a shotgun list of recycled claims, most of which the essays and apologetic work answer.

Genuinely arguable. The timeline is established, including Snow's own recorded explanation. Whether it was information control or pastoral prudence is a judgement call. The church did publish the material, and that counts. Runnells being disciplined for compiling questions sits awkwardly beside the transparency claim.
"When did you first read the Gospel Topics Essays? How did you come across them?"

september-six.d: In September 1993, six Mormon scholars and feminists were excommunicated or disfellowshipped within weeks of each other. Lavina Fielding Anderson. Avraham Gileadi. Maxine Hanks. D. Michael Quinn. Paul Toscano. Lynne Kanavel Whitesides.
History and theology that leaders did not welcome. Quinn's research on plural marriage after 1890. Writing about Heavenly Mother. Feminist advocacy.

Months before, the apostle Boyd K. Packer had named the church's three great dangers in public. They were "the gay-lesbian movement, the feminist movement, and the so-called scholars or intellectuals." On paper the discipline was local. The evidence points to apostles taking part. Mormon studies went quiet for a generation.

That discipline is run locally, by stake presidents. It is for conduct such as speaking out against the church and its leaders. That is apostasy as the handbook sets it out. It is not scholarship as such. Many working historians publish critical work and are never disciplined. And the church does not run these councils from the centre. FAIR also points to what came after: the Joseph Smith Papers, the Gospel Topics Essays, and Maxine Hanks being rebaptised in 2012.

Strong for you. The six actions, their timing and Packer's speech are on the record, and no one disputes them. Only the question of how much came from the centre is argued. As a claim about how the church met dissent, it stands.
"What happened to the six in 1993? I'd like to know how you read it."

sec-ensign-peak-settlement.d: On 21 February 2023 the Securities and Exchange Commission charged the church and its investment arm, Ensign Peak Advisors. The charge was failing to disclose. From 1997 to 2019, Ensign Peak hid a portfolio of listed shares behind 13 shell companies. Each had a manager in name only. The forms it filed, called Forms 13F, were wrong. The portfolio grew to about $32 billion.
To avoid revealing the church's holdings. The SEC order says this was done with the knowledge and approval of the First Presidency, out of concern about negative publicity.
Ensign Peak paid $4 million. The church paid $1 million. Note what this is and is not. It is a legal finding about candour. It says nothing about whether any doctrine is true.

The church says it took legal advice on how to meet the rules while keeping the portfolio private. It cites scripture on keeping sacred gifts quiet, and on not making a show. It says it regrets the mistakes made. When the SEC first raised a concern in 2019, Ensign Peak changed its filings at once. It now files one form for the whole fund. And note what the settlement did not allege. No misuse of funds. No fraud against investors. No harm to members.

They admit this themselves. The facts are fixed by the SEC order, and by the church's own statement owning the mistakes. The shell companies and the wish to avoid bad press are in the order. All that is left to argue is what to call it.
"Why thirteen shell companies? The order says it was about publicity."

tithing-enforcement.d: A temple recommend is required for the ordinances the church teaches are needed for exaltation. That includes attending your own child's temple wedding. The interview asks: "Are you a full-tithe payer?" And once a year members declare their status to the bishop. That meeting was called tithing settlement; since 2019 it is tithing declaration.
D&C 64:23 is canon: "he that is tithed shall not be burned at his coming." D&C 119:3-4 sets the standard. Leaders have taught paying tithing before feeding your family.
James Huntsman sued over how tithing was used. The full Ninth Circuit dismissed it 11 to 0 in January 2025. Do not repeat the fraud claim. It has been answered in court.

There is no paid local clergy. Bishops, teachers and leaders all serve free. Tithing pays for chapels, temples, education, operations and a large welfare and humanitarian programme. Members widely testify that paying it is a blessing rather than a burden. Tithing long predates this church; Malachi 3:8-10 calls withholding it robbing God, so gating on it has a biblical case. And the declaration is self-reported. Nobody audits your income.

They admit the structure, and none of it is contested. It is all in current church publications. The core point is simply a description: ordinances tied to salvation are conditioned on a financial contribution. Set that beside 2 Corinthians 9:7 — give "not grudgingly, or of necessity."
"What happens at the recommend interview if you say you haven't paid?"

missionary-program-realities.d: Men go at 18 for 24 months. Women go at 19 for 18 months. They work full-time and unpaid, and they pay to do it — a flat $500 a month since 2020, usually funded by the family.

Mission rules and a mission president set the schedule, the media allowed, and the rule that a companion is always present. Until February 2019, contact with family was weekly email plus two phone calls a year: Mother's Day and Christmas.
Cultural and family expectation to serve is strong. So is the stigma of coming home early. That is widely described by members themselves.

Service is voluntary, and it is framed as consecration rather than labour. The flat payment equalises it: a missionary in Tokyo pays what one in Peru pays, and ward funds cover those who cannot. Enormous numbers of returned missionaries call it the formative experience of their lives — a language, a discipline, a habit of service. The structure exists for safety and focus, as in monastic and military life. And the 2019 changes, with weekly calls and more flexible days, show the institution listening.

They admit all of it; every element comes from the church's own publications. The steelman is real too. It is voluntary, and the benefits people report are genuine. Calling it unpaid labour understates how much people choose it. This one is low stakes — mention it, do not press it.
"How often could you call home on your mission?"

jesus-lucifer-spirit-brothers.d: That Lucifer was a spirit son of God. In the council before this world, he offered a rival plan. Moses 4:1-4 has him say "Behold, here am I, send me, I will be thy son… wherefore give me thine honor." He was competing with the premortal Jesus. See Abraham 3:27-28, D&C 76:25-27, and Gospel Principles chapter 3.
Every being is a spirit child of the same Heavenly Father. So in that scheme, Jesus and Lucifer are elder and younger spirit brothers.

Mike Huckabee raised it in public. The church's Newsroom answered on 12 December 2007. It granted the underlying teaching and rejected the framing: all beings "were created by God and are his spirit children," while Satan "is a fallen angel."

FAIR calls the taxonomy technically accurate but the framing misleading. Shared parentage implies no parity. Cain and Abel were brothers, and nobody calls them equals. FAIR notes the Bible itself calls Satan one of the "sons of God" at Job 1:6 and 2:1. Jesus is uniquely the first and greatest Son, the Creator of this world, and the Only Begotten in the flesh. Satan squandered what he had. The 2007 statement says the two are "diametrically opposite" in every attribute.

Strong for you — but drop the crude version first. Nobody serious says Mormons think Jesus and the devil are alike. The real point is what kind of being each one is. Colossians 1:16 says by Christ were all things created, "whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers." Satan is in that list. Ezekiel 28:15 says of him "thou wast created." A potter and his pot are not brothers.
"Did Jesus make Satan, or are they the same kind of being?"

god-exalted-man-flesh-and-bone.d: D&C 130:22 is canon: "The Father has a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's." In the King Follett sermon of 1844 Joseph Smith preached that "God himself was once as we are now, and is an exalted man." The 2014 essay Becoming Like God still quotes that approvingly, with Lorenzo Snow's couplet. The same essay affirms that God organised the universe out of matter that already existed.

Brigham Young took it further. In 1852 he taught that "Adam is our father and our God, and the only God with whom we have to do." That is Journal of Discourses 1:50-51, and it entered the temple lecture at the veil in 1877. In October 1976, President Spencer W. Kimball denounced it in General Conference: "We denounce that theory… false doctrine."

John 4:24 — "God is a Spirit." Numbers 23:19 — "God is not a man." Psalm 90:2 — "from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God." Isaiah 43:10 — "before me there was no God formed." Hebrews 11:3 has the worlds framed by the word of God. Malachi 3:6 and Hosea 11:9 point the same way.

FAIR reads John 4:24 as mode and character, not anatomy. Compare "God is light" in 1 John 1:5 and "a consuming fire" in Deuteronomy 4:24. Nobody treats those as the whole story. Spirit and body are not opposites either; the risen Christ has flesh and bone in Luke 24:39. FAIR points to appearances of God in Exodus 33:11 and 33:23. And David Paulsen of BYU argues the earliest Christians thought of God in bodily terms, before Greek philosophy displaced it. On Adam-God, FAIR says Young was poorly recorded or misunderstood, that it was never canonised, and that the church correcting it shows living prophets working.

Strong for you. Every part is documented in canon or in current church publications. Take the verses together rather than one at a time. A God who was once as we are cannot be God from everlasting to everlasting. And the Adam-God episode cuts hard against the self-correction defence. One prophet formally called another prophet's pulpit teaching about God false doctrine.
"Psalm 90:2 says from everlasting to everlasting. Was there a time he was not God?"

different-jesus-hinckley-1998.d: He was asked in 1998 whether Latter-day Saints believe in "the traditional Christ." The church president answered: "No, I don't. The traditional Christ of whom they speak is not the Christ of whom I speak. For the Christ of whom I speak has been revealed in this the Dispensation of the Fulness of Times." It is in the Church News of 20 June 1998.
Because it is the sitting prophet naming the difference himself. Paul warns about "another Jesus, whom we have not preached" in 2 Corinthians 11:4, and another gospel in Galatians 1:8.

FAIR says the quote is real but misused. In context Hinckley was contrasting their Christ with the creedal Christ. That is the Christ of Nicaea and Chalcedon, the being with no body. He was not contrasting him with the Jesus of the New Testament. Latter-day Saints insist they worship that Jesus as divine Son, Saviour and Redeemer. The Living Christ, from 2000, says so. The essay Are Mormons Christian? adds that early Christian views of God shifted a great deal under Greek thought. And on 2 Corinthians 11:4, Paul was after a different message, not a test in metaphysics.

Genuinely arguable, and do not rest your case on this quote. The quotation is real, and the difference is real. But "traditional Christ" most naturally means the creeds. FAIR's point has force there. Whether the same man with a different metaphysics counts as another Jesus is a question for the doctrinal cases. One sentence will not settle it.
"When Hinckley said 'not the traditional Christ,' what did you understand him to mean?"

premortal-spirit-children.d: That every human lived before birth as a literal spirit child of Heavenly Parents. The essay Mother in Heaven says all human beings "are beloved spirit children of heavenly parents." A First Presidency statement of 1909, quoted in Gospel Principles chapter 2, says man as a spirit "was begotten and born of heavenly parents." Abraham 3:22-23 describes intelligences organised before the world. See also D&C 93:29 and Moses 3:5.

1 Corinthians 15:46 puts the order the other way: "that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural." Zechariah 12:1 says the LORD "formeth the spirit of man within him." And in Genesis 2:7 man becomes a living soul when God breathes into formed dust.

FAIR builds a real biblical case. God knew Jeremiah "before I formed thee in the belly" at Jeremiah 1:5. The sons of God "shouted for joy" when the earth was founded, in Job 38:4-7. At death the spirit "shall return unto God who gave it," in Ecclesiastes 12:7 — and return implies having been there. Hebrews 12:9 calls God "the Father of spirits." The disciples' question in John 9:2 seems to allow for it. Origen held that souls existed before bodies, before the church condemned it in the sixth century. And on 1 Corinthians 15:46 they say Paul is talking about resurrection bodies.

Strong for you, and give them one point. FAIR is right that 1 Corinthians 15:46 is about resurrection bodies, so do not lean on it. The rest dissolves in context. Jeremiah 1:5 is about God choosing, as in Romans 8:29. The sons of God in Job 38:7 are angels, and God's whole point is that Job was not there. Ecclesiastes 12:7 pairs with dust going back to earth. And Origen taught nothing like heavenly parents giving birth to spirits. That specific claim has no biblical support at all.
"Which verse says our spirits were born to heavenly parents?"

trinity-vs-godhead.d: That the Father, Son and Holy Ghost are three separate beings, one in purpose but not one being. The Father and the Son have tangible bodies; see D&C 130:22 and the Gospel Topics page on the Godhead. Joseph Smith—History 1:19 has God call all existing creeds "an abomination in his sight." Abraham 4:1 has creation carried out by "the Gods." And Smith preached a plurality of gods openly in the Sermon in the Grove, in June 1844.

Deuteronomy 6:4 — "The LORD our God is one LORD." Isaiah 44:24 is sharper still. God stretches out the heavens "alone" and spreads the earth "by myself." No council of gods. 1 Corinthians 8:4 says "there is none other God but one."
The Book of Mormon reads like the Bible here. Alma 11:28-29 asks whether there is more than one God, and answers no. 2 Nephi 31:21 says the same.

And this is the strongest set they have. First, John 17:22: Jesus prays that believers "may be one, even as we are one." Believers do not merge into one substance. So the oneness in that same sentence reads as relational. Second, Jesus is visibly distinct from the Father all through the New Testament. At his baptism. In Gethsemane. In Stephen's vision at Acts 7:55-56. And 1 Corinthians 8:6 distinguishes one God the Father from one Lord Jesus Christ. Third, respected Christian philosophers model the Trinity as three centres of mind in one essence and will. Alvin Plantinga, Richard Swinburne and William Lane Craig all do. BYU scholars argue that lands near the Godhead. Fourth, Psalm 82 has plural elohim language native to the Old Testament.

Genuinely arguable, and the John 17 reading is fair. Do not pretend otherwise. The difference shows where the doctrine goes further. Those philosophers still hold one uncreated divine essence. Here there are three independent beings, two with bodies, at least one of whom became divine — and exaltation hands godhood to others. Isaiah 44:24 and 43:10 exclude that.
"Isaiah 44:24 says he made everything alone. Who else was there?"

adam-god-doctrine.d: On 9 April 1852, in general conference, he taught that Adam "is our Father and our God, and the only God with whom we have to do." It is in Journal of Discourses 1:50-51.

Over two decades. In 1873 he said that "Adam is my father" was doctrine God had revealed to him. In 1877 he had it put into the temple lecture at the veil in the St George Temple. L. John Nuttall recorded that in his journal on 7 February 1877.

Genesis 2:7, where Adam is a creature formed by God. Hosea 11:9, where God is not a man. And Latter-day Saint scripture itself: D&C 27:11 and 107:53-55 identify Adam as the archangel Michael, who is under God.
In 1976 President Spencer W. Kimball told general conference: "the Adam-God theory… We denounce that theory and hope that everyone will be cautioned against this and other kinds of false doctrine."

FAIR says Young's sermons survive only in imperfect transcriptions. It says he taught other things that do not fit a strong Adam-God reading. And it says the teaching was never canonised by common consent, so it was one man's speculation rather than church doctrine. Kimball's denunciation is presented as the system working: the living church corrects itself, and doctrine is set by scripture and the united voice of the First Presidency, not by every pulpit statement of a past president.
"Kimball called it false doctrine. Brigham Young taught it in the temple. How do you hold both?"

lorenzo-snow-couplet-status.d: "As man now is, God once was; as God now is, man may be." Lorenzo Snow wrote it in 1840. Joseph Smith's King Follett sermon of 1844 ratified it. Prophets and manuals have taught it ever since. The Teachings of the Presidents: Lorenzo Snow manual features it.

In 1997 Richard Ostling of Time asked President Hinckley whether God the Father was once a man. He answered: "I don't know that we teach it. I don't know that we emphasize it… I understand the philosophical background behind it, but I don't know a lot about it." He told the San Francisco Chronicle it was "more of a couplet than anything else."
Becoming Like God affirms the second half firmly. People may become like God. It handles the first half — God's own past as a man — with studied vagueness.

That Hinckley was answering narrowly. The church does not emphasise or elaborate the doctrine, because little has been revealed about it. He was not denying it. At the next General Conference he said the news reports had been incomplete. And the 2014 essay does affirm that humans may become like God, while noting that scripture says little about God's past.

Strong for you, and note what it is about. This case is not about the doctrine itself; that is covered elsewhere. It is about candour. The same church that publishes a manual built around the couplet had its prophet tell national media "I don't know that we teach it." Ronald Huggins traced its use in church curricula in the Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society in 2006. Most members have learned it. Showing them that answer tends to land.
"Have you seen what President Hinckley told Time magazine about the couplet?"

facsimile-1-lion-couch.t: What Joseph Smith said it shows
facsimile-1-lion-couch.d: Abraham "fastened upon an altar." Over him, "the idolatrous priest of Elkenah attempting to offer up Abraham as a sacrifice." That is his own printed explanation, figures 2 and 3. Abraham 1:12-15 tells the story.

A standard funeral scene. The original survives as Papyrus Joseph Smith I. It is part of the Book of Breathings made for a Theban priest named Hor, around the second or first century BC. That is more than 1,500 years after Abraham. The scene shows the jackal-headed god Anubis tending the dead man on a lion couch.

The papyrus has a hole. It sits exactly where the priest's head and the knife appear in the 1842 woodcut. The woodcut shows a bald human head and a raised knife. Robert Ritner and others note ink traces of a headdress at the shoulder, which points to Anubis. And no other scene of this kind has a knife in it.

John Gee, Kerry Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central make four points. Nobody knows what filled the hole, so a human head and a knife could have been there. This scene is unusual: the figure on the couch looks alive and clothed, with both hands perhaps raised. Egyptian temple texts do show ritual killing of enemies, so a sacrifice reading is not absurd. Jews living in Egypt did reuse Egyptian pictures for their own stories. And the catalyst view says the papyri only prompted revelation, so the explanations are inspired comment rather than translation.

Genuinely arguable, unlike the other two facsimiles. The hole covers the very things in dispute, so the case runs on parallels and ink traces. The Egyptological reading is far better supported, and the church's own essay grants that Egyptologists read it differently. But note the rest. The canopic jars as gods of foreign nations, and the crocodile as the god of Pharaoh, have no support at all.
"What do you make of the missing piece? That's where the whole argument sits."

facsimile-2-hypocephalus.d: A hypocephalus. That is a round funeral amulet, laid under the head of a mummy. It comes from spell 162 of the Book of the Dead, and this one was made for a man named Sheshonq. Its purpose was to keep the dead warm and help them rise.

facsimile-2-hypocephalus.t: What Joseph Smith said it means
facsimile-2-hypocephalus.d: Cosmology. Figure 1 is "Kolob, signifying the first creation, nearest to the celestial, or the residence of God." Figure 5 is the sun, receiving light through a medium he calls Kae-e-vanrash. Abraham 3:2-4 and 3:9 go with it.

Egyptologists all identify it as Min, a fertility god. He is shown seated, with an erect phallus and a raised flail, approached by a serpent. Smith labelled it "God sitting upon his throne, revealing through the heavens the grand Key-words of the Priesthood." His explanation goes on: "as, also, the sign of the Holy Ghost unto Abraham, in the form of a dove."

Michael Rhodes is a Latter-day Saint scholar. His own translation of the rim and panels gives ordinary funeral prayers for Sheshonq. Parts of the original were missing in 1842 and were filled in with characters copied from other papyri, including lines from Hor's Book of Breathings.

Rhodes, John Gee, Kerry Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central grant that figure 7 is a form of Min. They argue three things. To Egyptians, Min was a supreme creator god. He stood for the power that makes life. So "God sitting upon his throne" may catch his role, even if the image startles us. Second, hypocephali are esoteric objects about cosmic geography and rebirth. A cosmological reading is not alien to that genre. Some argue that figure 4, as the firmament, lands near an Egyptian idea. Third, under the catalyst view, the explanations were never meant as decipherment at all.
"Even the church's own scholars say figure 7 is Min. What do you do with that?"

facsimile-3-presentation.t: Why this one is the cleanest test
facsimile-3-presentation.d: The captions survive. Facsimile 1 has a hole in it. Here the hieroglyphs beside each figure are printed in the woodcut, and Egyptologists can read them.
A standard presentation vignette from the Book of Breathings of the priest Hor. The dead man Hor is led by Maat and Anubis, and presented to Osiris on his throne, with Isis behind him.

Robert Ritner translated them. Figure 2, which Smith called "King Pharaoh, whose name is given in the characters above his head," is captioned "Isis the great, the god's mother." A goddess. Figure 4, which Smith called "Prince of Pharaoh, King of Egypt," is "Maat, mistress of the gods." Also a goddess. Figure 1, Smith's Abraham on the throne, is Osiris. Figure 5, Smith's "Shulem, one of the king's principal waiters," is "The Osiris Hor, justified forever" — the owner of the papyrus. Figure 6, Smith's slave Olimlah, is Anubis.
Théodule Devéria reached the same conclusions in 1860. So did the 1912 panel of Egyptologists, which included Flinders Petrie and James Breasted. They worked independently.

It does not offer a rival translation. Gee, Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central accept the readings and argue for relabelling. In Egyptian thought Pharaoh embodied Osiris on earth, and Isis could be identified with the throne itself, so Isis as Pharaoh has some precedent. Jews in Egypt did adapt Egyptian scenes for their own figures, and Abraham turns up in later Egyptian magical texts. Presentation scenes do dress figures in one another's imagery. And some caption glyphs are poorly copied in the woodcut.
"He said the name is written above the head. It's written. It says Isis."

egyptian-alphabet-grammar.d: The working papers. Alongside the Book of Abraham, Joseph Smith's circle produced the Kirtland Egyptian Papers. Among them is a bound volume, Grammar and Alphabet of the Egyptian Language, from 1835. It is in the hands of W. W. Phelps and Warren Parrish. The Joseph Smith Papers have published it in full.
That he was "studying the Egyptian language." And that the group was "engaged in translating an alphabet to the Book of Abraham, and arranging a grammar of the Egyptian language."

It gives a single Egyptian character a paragraph of English meaning. Those meanings then multiply through five degrees. Egyptologists reject it entirely. It bears no relation to Egyptian. And three Book of Abraham manuscripts have characters copied in order from the Hor papyrus down the margin, beside the English.

Gee, Muhlestein and Pearl of Great Price Central argue the dependence runs the other way. The scribes were trying to work backwards from an English text already revealed. It was an exercise Joseph allowed but did not write. Most pages are in scribes' handwriting. The grammar was never published or canonised. And they argue the Abraham text came first, on textual grounds.

Genuinely arguable on the narrow question. Which came first is really debated, and the Joseph Smith Papers editors call the documents intertwined. But the escape is expensive. His own journal says he was arranging the grammar. Either way, his circle produced an Egyptian system, under his eye, that is nonsense. Use it to support the papyri case, not on its own.
"Have you seen the Egyptian alphabet they made in Kirtland? It's published."

endowment-masonic-origins.d: Joseph Smith was initiated into Freemasonry at Nauvoo on 15 and 16 March 1842. He rose to Master Mason in a single day. Seven weeks later, on 4 May 1842, he introduced the temple endowment. The first nine men to receive it were all Masons. The church's own history essay acknowledges this.

Tokens, which are grips. Signs. Key words. Ritual penalties miming the cutting of the throat and the opening of the body. The five points of fellowship. And the compass and square. The penalty oaths and the five points were removed from the ceremony in April 1990.
This is sacred to the person you are talking to. Do not smirk about it, and do not ask them to describe what they covenanted not to describe. Ask about the history, which is public.

The church and FAIR grant the parallels and separate form from substance. Masonry was a catalyst for revelation — a familiar ritual language Joseph used to teach covenants that were genuinely revealed. The content has no Masonic counterpart: creation, fall, redemption, and covenants of consecration. Unlike Masonry it was given to women, and to the weakest of the Saints. The ritual is the vehicle, not the endowment itself, so revising it in 1990 and 2019 is continuing revelation rather than damage control. And the temple is sacred, not secret. The teachings are published; only certain signs and tokens are withheld, as Jesus held some things back in Mark 4:34 and John 16:12.

They admit the facts, and the catalyst reading is a fair theological move. It interprets those facts; it does not deny them. Notice one thing. The older apologetic — that the endowment was preserved from Solomon's temple — has quietly been dropped. Set the dates beside John 18:20, where Jesus says "in secret have I said nothing."
"He became a Mason in March and gave the endowment in May. How do you read those dates?"

avoid-worship-joseph-smith.d: That Mormons worship Joseph Smith. Usually with the hymn as evidence — Hymn 27, Praise to the Man.

Latter-day Saints worship God the Father and Jesus Christ. The church denies worshipping Smith, plainly and often. Members hear the charge as an obvious misreading of their own lives. The hymn honours a founder. Its language is extravagant — "mingling with Gods" — but it is not worship.
Open with this and you are wrong in your first sentence. It is corrected in ten seconds. And it marks you as someone who has never actually sat with a Latter-day Saint.

avoid-worship-joseph-smith.t: What is true and useful instead
avoid-worship-joseph-smith.d: Everything distinctive here rests on one man's claims. Joseph Fielding Smith wrote it himself: "Mormonism, as it is called, must stand or fall on the story of Joseph Smith." That is Doctrines of Salvation 1:188. Their own leader opened that door.
Do not use it as stated. Use what is behind it. The test is whether Joseph told the truth, and the church agrees that is the test.
"I know you worship Christ. But every distinctive doctrine rests on Joseph. Can we test that?"

avoid-coca-cola-ownership.d: That the church secretly owns Coca-Cola, or Pepsi. Usually with a joke about banning caffeine while selling it.

It is an urban legend. Snopes traced it to how neat the irony sounds. No such stake has ever existed. And Ensign Peak's public filings, after the SEC settlement, list no Coca-Cola, no PepsiCo and no Keurig Dr Pepper. The legend also rests on a second error, since the church never banned caffeine.
Repeating a legend that Snopes debunked hands your friend a free win. It also taints everything true you say afterwards.

The real finance story is far stronger, and it is admitted. Ensign Peak held a reserve of more than $100 billion, kept quiet. In 2023 the SEC settled charges over hiding about $32 billion behind shell companies. That case is on this site, and it needs no legend.
Do not use it. If church money is the subject, go to the SEC settlement. It is adjudicated fact.
"Forget the Coke rumour. Have you read what the SEC found in 2023?"

avoid-magic-underwear-mockery.d: "Magic underwear." Any version of it. Any tone.

The garment is real, and the practice is documented — that case is on this site. But this phrase is mockery, not argument. The church's 2014 video Sacred Temple Clothing answers it directly. It compares the garment to a nun's habit, a prayer shawl and a monk's robe, and calls the phrase inaccurate and offensive. Folk beliefs about physical protection do exist among members. They are not doctrine.

You become the aggressor. You trigger the persecution frame the church has already made a video about. And you throw away the point you were reaching for. 1 Peter 3:15-16 tells us to answer with meekness and fear, and Colossians 4:6 says let your speech be with grace.

It is not about fabric. It is about enforcement. Wearing the garment is checked in the temple recommend interview. Until recently, women's garment norms were policed in some detail. That is a question about religious control, and you can ask it respectfully.
Do not use it, ever. Ask, do not jeer. This is sacred to the person in front of you, and it is personal.
"How did it feel to have an interview cover your underwear?"

avoid-white-horse-prophecy.d: That the White Horse Prophecy is Latter-day Saint doctrine. That a Mormon will ride in and save the Constitution when it hangs by a thread, and that Mormon politicians think they are the one.

The church repudiated it officially in 2010. Its statement says the story is "based on accounts that have not been substantiated by historical research and is not embraced as Church doctrine." The full text is a secondhand recollection from 1902, of doubtful origin.
Cite it as doctrine and your friend quotes the 2010 statement back at you. The conversation is over, and you handed them the ending.

The narrower teaching is genuinely attested. That the Constitution will hang by a thread, and the elders will save it. Brigham Young taught it. So did John Taylor — see Journal of Discourses 7:15. Modern leaders invoked it too, including Ezra Taft Benson.
Do not lead with White Horse. Lead with the thread quotes. Those came from prophets' own mouths in documented sermons, and cannot be waved off as folklore.
"Brigham Young said the Constitution would hang by a thread. What did he mean?"

avoid-caffeine-ban.d: That Mormons are not allowed caffeine. No Coke. No Dr Pepper.

The Word of Wisdom's "hot drinks" at D&C 89:9 has been officially read as coffee and tea only. In 2012 the church stated that it "does not prohibit the use of caffeine." BYU has sold caffeinated soda since 2017. Many faithful members drink Coke. And caffeine appears nowhere in a temple recommend interview.
Getting this wrong signals that you learned Mormonism from playground rumour. Everything after it gets discounted.

avoid-caffeine-ban.t: What is actually strange, stated correctly
avoid-caffeine-ban.d: Iced coffee bars you from the temple, while a quadruple-shot energy drink does not. The canonised text calls itself "not by commandment or constraint" at D&C 89:2, and became a test of worthiness decades later. And "hot drinks" meaning exactly coffee and tea is itself a later interpretation.
Do not use it as stated. Ask why the line falls where it does. Do not misstate where the line is. The Word of Wisdom case on this site carries the argument.
"Why is iced coffee a problem and an energy drink isn't?"

avoid-own-planet.d: That good Mormons each get their own planet when they die.

The 2014 essay Becoming Like God loaded the rebuttal in advance. It says exaltation gets "reduced in media to a cartoonish image of people receiving their own planets." A church FAQ answers the planet question with a flat no. Say it and your friend hands you the essay.

And the church affirms it. Exaltation means becoming gods. D&C 132:20 says "then shall they be gods." It includes eternal increase and a share in creation. Past leaders said it in cosmic terms — Lorenzo Snow, Brigham Young, and Spencer W. Kimball, who spoke of creating worlds. Moses 1:33 has worlds without number.

avoid-own-planet.t: Use their words, not South Park's
avoid-own-planet.d: Quote D&C 132:20 and set Isaiah beside it. Isaiah 43:10 — "before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me." Isaiah 44:6-8 says the same.
Do not use the phrase. The doctrine underneath it is fully conceded, so the only error is the packaging. Fixing the packaging is free. The exaltation case on this site carries the full argument.
"Your scripture says the exalted shall be gods. Isaiah says none will be formed after him. Can both be true?"

avoid-1826-convicted-conman.d: That Joseph Smith was a convicted con man. That a court convicted him of fraud in 1826, just before he found the plates.
The 1826 Bainbridge proceeding was real. Smith was 20. He was charged as a "disorderly person" over paid glass looking. Justice Neely's own fee bill calls him "The Glass Looker."

It was probably a preliminary examination, not a trial. The surviving records are fragmentary and they contradict each other. The Pearsall account says guilty. The fee bill and mittimus evidence point the other way. Scholars split — Gordon Madsen reads it as a discharge, while Dan Vogel and Wesley Walters disagree. Convicted states as fact what the documents cannot carry.

The occupation. By the church's own Gospel Topics essay, and by Richard Bushman in Rough Stone Rolling, Smith was a paid treasure-seer. He hunted buried valuables by looking at a stone in his hat. It was the same stone, in the same hat, that produced the Book of Mormon.
Do not lead with it, and never say convicted. Lead with the seer-stone facts the church admits, which are in the translation case. Then let the 1826 record confirm the timeline.
"The 1826 papers call him 'The Glass Looker.' Same stone, same hat, a few years later."

prophetic-fallibility-unfalsifiable.t: What prophets have taught and the church later dropped
prophetic-fallibility-unfalsifiable.d: Brigham Young said the moon and the sun are inhabited. That is Journal of Discourses 13:271, from 1870. He also taught Adam-God in general conference, which Spencer W. Kimball later denounced as false doctrine. And Bruce R. McConkie's Mormon Doctrine, from 1958, needed more than 1,000 corrections after apostles reviewed it. It sold for decades, and was pulled in 2010.
Wilford Woodruff's declaration sits with Official Declaration 1 in the canon. "The Lord will never permit me or any other man who stands as President of this Church to lead you astray."
It makes a loop that nothing can test. Whatever a prophet teaches is prophetic, until it is not. Then it becomes opinion, after the fact.

And much of it lands. The church teaches openly that prophets are fallible men. Joseph Smith said a prophet is only a prophet when acting as such, and not every sermon is revelation. Young flagged the moon and sun remark as speculation — "I rather think it is" — and it matched the science of his day; William Herschel thought the sun inhabited. It was never canonised. Mormon Doctrine was a private book McConkie published without permission, so its correction shows the system working. And Woodruff was answering a specific fear, that the Manifesto was apostasy.

Genuinely arguable, and pick your example carefully. The moon quote and Mormon Doctrine are weak, and you will be corrected on both. Adam-God is the strong one, because it was taught in conference and later disavowed. The unfalsifiable-loop point is fair philosophy. It is not a failed prophecy.
"How would you tell the difference between a prophet's revelation and his opinion?"

kirtland-safety-society.d: In November 1836 Joseph Smith helped found a bank. It was called the Kirtland Safety Society. Ohio refused it a charter. So in January 1837 it changed its name, to the Kirtland Safety Society Anti-Banking Company. Then it issued its notes anyway.

On 6 January 1837, Wilford Woodruff wrote in his journal that Smith had "receieved that morning the word of the Lord upon the subject of the Kirtland Safety Society." Not only by the spirit, he wrote, "but even an audaible voice." If the commandments were heeded, all would be well. Warren Parrish, an officer who later left, claimed Smith prophesied it would swallow up all other banks like Aaron's rod.

The bank had far too little capital behind it. Its notes lost most of their value within weeks. On 24 October 1837 Smith and Sidney Rigdon were each fined $1,000 and costs for illegal banking, under an Ohio statute of 1816. Smith fled Kirtland on the night of 12 January 1838.

Historians put the loss at 200 to 300 members. That is roughly 10 to 15% of Kirtland. It took about a third of the top leaders with it. Heber C. Kimball later said that for every member who stood by Joseph Smith as prophet, "there were twenty who did not."

FAIR and church historians make five points. The 1830s was the age of wild, unwatched banking. Hundreds of banks went down in the Panic of 1837. The charter was refused partly for Ohio party reasons; hard-money Democrats turned down nearly every new charter that year. Smith put in more of his own money than almost anyone, and lost it — not what a swindler does. He resigned in June 1837, and warned the Saints about the notes. And Woodruff never wrote down what the revelation said. The grand line about swallowing up all banks comes only from Parrish, who by then had left and was hostile.
"Woodruff wrote that he heard an audible voice about the bank. What do you make of that?"

priesthood-restoration-late-account.d: That John the Baptist restored the Aaronic priesthood in May 1829, and that Peter, James and John restored the Melchizedek priesthood soon after. See D&C 13 and Joseph Smith—History 1:68-72.

priesthood-restoration-late-account.t: When it first appears in writing
priesthood-restoration-late-account.d: October 1834. Oliver Cowdery's account in the Messenger and Advocate. That is five years later. Joseph's own 1832 history does not narrate it. The 1833 Book of Commandments has none of the passages.

The text was expanded. What is now D&C 27 began as a short 1830 revelation. It grew into a longer one that names John the Baptist, and Peter, James and John. Compare Book of Commandments 28. Both are on the Joseph Smith Papers site.
David Whitmer told interviewers he never heard that an angel had ordained Joseph and Oliver to the Aaronic priesthood until years after 1830. William McLellin said the same.

FAIR and BYU scholars reply on four fronts. The 1832 history does mention receiving "the holy Priesthood by the ministring of Aangels." An 1829-era revelation, now D&C 27, points to authority from heavenly messengers. Joseph and Oliver kept the details quiet because of persecution; Joseph said they were "forced to keep secret the circumstances of having received the Priesthood." The 1835 additions are a prophet making his own earlier words clearer. And Whitmer and McLellin were hostile by then, recalling events forty or fifty years on.
"When is the first written account that names the angels? I'd like to read it."

book-of-commandments-revisions.d: Revelations printed in 1833 as the word of God were rewritten for the 1835 Doctrine and Covenants. Hundreds of changes, some of them substantive. You can check every one in the church's own Joseph Smith Papers scans.

Book of Commandments 4:2 says God "will grant him no other gift." D&C 5:4 makes it "no other gift until it is finished." Book of Commandments 7 says Oliver Cowdery's gift is working with the rod, the rod of nature. D&C 8 renames the divining rod "the gift of Aaron." And Book of Commandments 28 grew into eighteen verses, now D&C 27. Those verses name the angels who restored the priesthood.

Deuteronomy 4:2 and Proverbs 30:5-6 forbid adding to God's words. Look at what these edits imply. A text says thus saith the Lord. Then it has to be re-engineered years later, to fit how the movement grew. That looks like a human draft.

FAIR says Joseph never claimed word-for-word dictation. Revelations came as impressions, put into his own imperfect language. So the prophet who received them could revise and expand them as the church grew and his understanding grew. The additions to section 20 simply took in offices revealed after 1830. The church publishes every version openly, which is the opposite of concealment. And the revised texts were accepted by common consent at the 1835 conference.

They admit this themselves, and publish both editions side by side. The defence justifies the edits; it does not deny them. Notice the price. If revelations are fallible paraphrases that can be re-engineered later, then every thus saith the Lord weighs less — including D&C 132.
"Have you compared the 1833 and 1835 versions? They're both on the church's own site."

zelph-white-lamanite.d: On 3 June 1834, during Zion's Camp, Joseph Smith's men dug into a burial mound near the Illinois River. They found a skeleton with an arrowhead between its ribs. The site is Naples-Russell Mound 8, in Pike County, Illinois. It is a Hopewell burial.

That by vision the bones belonged to "Zelph," a white Lamanite warrior-chief who served under "the great prophet Onandagus." He had been killed in battle. Several accounts add that Onandagus was known from the Rocky Mountains to the eastern sea.
At least six men who were there. Wilford Woodruff. Heber C. Kimball. George A. Smith. Levi Hancock. Moses Martin. Reuben McBride. The story entered History of the Church 2:79-80.

FAIR draws on Kenneth Godfrey's source study. Joseph wrote nothing about Zelph himself. The six diaries disagree on details — which battle it was, and whether the Rocky Mountains line was original. The version in History of the Church is a later scribal blend that turned a campfire remark into formal revelation. And even at face value, apologists say Zelph could be a late Lamanite far from the core lands, so it fixes nothing about geography.

Genuinely arguable on the details. The accounts do differ, and the printed version is a conflation. But all six diaries agree on the core. Joseph claimed a vision naming a specific skeleton as a white Lamanite under a prophet called Onandagus. Either that is a false revelatory claim about a Hopewell burial, or it has to be downgraded to speculation.
"Six men wrote down the Zelph story that week. What do you do with it?"

bom-geography-retreat.t: What was taught for a century
bom-geography-retreat.d: A hemispheric Book of Mormon. Canonised revelations name North American Indians as Lamanites. See D&C 28:8, 32:2 and 54:8. Joseph Smith pointed at ruins in Central America, in the Times and Seasons in 1842. He pointed at sites in North America too. And the New York hill where he got the plates was the Cumorah of the last battles, in Mormon 6:6.
Joseph Fielding Smith warned that a second Cumorah would leave members "confused and disturbed in their faith." Marion Romney backed the New York hill in general conference, in 1975.

Under pressure from archaeology and DNA, scholars retreated to limited-geography models. Two camps now argue with each other. The Mesoamerican one, at FAIR and Scripture Central. And the Heartland one, at Rod Meldrum's FIRM Foundation. Each publishes detailed refutations of the other.
In 2019 a Gospel Topics statement said the church "does not take a position on the specific geographic locations." It asked members not to teach any geography in church settings.

Strong for you. This one leans on the digging and the DNA cases, so use it with them. Their answer is that the text never names a modern place. So the whole-hemisphere view was a habit of mind, not revelation. But the D&C is scripture, and it names North American tribes as Lamanites. Here is the telling part. Believers now take apart each other's maps, using the same arguments critics use.
"Where did it happen? Even the church says it takes no position."

holocaust-proxy-baptisms.d: Members performed proxy baptisms for hundreds of thousands of Holocaust victims. Jewish organisations protested. In 1995 the church signed an agreement to remove the names and stop, except for members' own direct ancestors.

The researcher Helen Radkey documented violations for two decades. Anne Frank's name was submitted at least a dozen times, and the ordinance performed at least nine times. One was at the Santo Domingo Temple in February 2012, and the church condemned it. Early in 2012, Simon Wiesenthal's parents were baptised by proxy. The church apologised formally to the family.

D&C 128:15 says the dead "cannot be made perfect" without our ordinances, and that this work is "essential to our salvation." It rests on one disputed verse, 1 Corinthians 15:29. Against it stand Hebrews 9:27, where judgment follows death, and Luke 16:26, where a fixed gulf separates the dead. Alma 34:32-35 makes the same point.

That proxy baptism compels nobody. The teaching is that the dead may accept or reject it, so it is an offering rather than a conversion. The institution honoured the 1995 agreement, and each documented violation was an individual member acting against explicit policy. And the church acted: names removed, database blocks engineered in 2010, apologies made to families, and warnings that violators lose temple privileges or face discipline.

They admit this themselves. The practice, the agreement, the years of violations, and the apologies are all conceded. The individual-members defence is fair as far as it goes. It also concedes the systemic point. A doctrine that makes this work essential to salvation creates a pressure that policy could not hold for twenty years. Handle it gently; these are real families.
"Hebrews 9:27 says judgment comes after death. How do the temple ordinances fit that?"

prop-8-campaign.d: On 29 June the First Presidency had a letter read from every California pulpit. It urged members to "do all you can" — their "means and time" — to pass Proposition 8. That measure stripped same-sex marriage out of California law.

Ward and stake structures became a precinct operation. Assigned donation targets. Phone banks. Door-to-door canvassing. All coordinated with the Protect Marriage coalition, which the church joined at the invitation of the Catholic Archbishop Niederauer.

Members gave an estimated $20 million, roughly half the funds of the Yes campaign. Latter-day Saints were about 2% of Californians. The church reported in-kind contributions, and was later fined by the California Fair Political Practices Commission for reporting them late. The same playbook had run in Hawaii in 1998, and on Proposition 22 in 2000.

That churches have always had the right, and a duty, to speak on moral questions. Marriage is a moral question, not a partisan one, and the church endorsed no candidate or party. It joined a broad interfaith coalition — Catholics, evangelicals, Orthodox Jews, Muslims — rather than acting alone. Direct institutional spending was small and disclosed. Members gave freely as private citizens. And D&C 134 also says governments should protect freedom of conscience.

They admit the facts, and their answer justifies the involvement rather than denying it. Be careful here. Christians themselves disagree about religious political advocacy, so the general charge will not land. Two narrower things do. D&C 134:9 says "we do not believe it just to mingle religious influence with civil government." And the pattern goes mobilise, then soften — Proposition 8, then the 2015 policy, then the 2019 reversal, then support for the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act.
"How do you read D&C 134:9 against what happened in 2008?"

huntsman-tithing-lawsuit.d: In 2021 James Huntsman sued the church for fraud, asking for about $5 million of tithing back. He quoted President Hinckley's assurance in general conference in 2003 about the City Creek mall: "tithing funds have not and will not be used to acquire this property." Against that he set the whistleblower David Nielsen, who said Ensign Peak Advisors moved about $1.4 billion toward City Creek.

A Ninth Circuit panel revived the claim in 2023. Then, on 31 January 2025, the full court ruled for the church, 11 to 0. Six judges held no reasonable juror could find misrepresentation. Hinckley in the same talk had said the money would come from "commercial entities owned by the Church" and from "earnings of invested reserve funds." The other judges would have barred the suit under church autonomy.

It is the one the court accepted. Hinckley's full 2003 statement distinguished tithing itself from earnings on invested reserves and from commercial-entity money. City Creek was funded from the latter. So there was no misrepresentation, and Huntsman produced no evidence that tithing principal was spent. The concurring judges added that the First Amendment bars civil courts from judging what a church tells members about sacred donations at all.

Do not use this one. After full argument the fraud theory lost 11 to 0, and for most of the judges it lost on the merits. Hinckley's own wording anticipated the distinction. What is left is whether earnings on invested tithing are still tithing, which is a quarrel about words. Cite this as proof of fraud and you will lose your credibility.
Nothing about this case. If money comes up, go to the SEC settlement, which is admitted fact.

paul-h-dunn-fabrications.d: Paul H. Dunn, a General Authority and a Seventy from 1964 to 1989. He was one of the church's most loved speakers, with bestselling books.
The war stories and the baseball stories. His best friend did not die in his arms in the Second World War. He never played for the St Louis Cardinals.

Lynn Packer investigated. The Arizona Republic published it in February 1991. Dunn at first defended the stories. They were needed, he said, "to illustrate his theological and moral points." Leaders had known earlier. Packer's reporting was held back. Meanwhile Dunn was quietly made emeritus in 1989, "for reasons of age and health."

In October 1991 he published a confession in the Church News. "I have not always been accurate in my public talks and writings." He acknowledged that the First Presidency and the Twelve had censured him.

They admit this themselves, and the church's own paper reported both halves. FAIR is right that one leader's sins do not falsify a religion. A dishonest pastor does not disprove Protestantism either. So use it small. What it does show is how faith-promoting stories work. Strong feelings get taken as confirmation. And it shows a taste for quiet management, until a journalist forced the issue.
"How would you know if a story that moved you wasn't true?"

hofmann-forgeries-church-response.d: Between 1980 and 1985 he supplied a stream of faked founding-era documents. The Anthon transcript in 1980. The Joseph Smith III blessing in 1981, quietly traded to the RLDS church. And in 1984 the salamander letter, in which "Martin Harris" describes a white salamander, not an angel, guarding the plates. Steve Christensen bought that one for $40,000 and gave it to the church.

Senior leaders, including Gordon B. Hinckley, met Hofmann repeatedly and acquired sensitive items. Some were held in the First Presidency vault. Leaders publicly played down what the church held. No apostle, seer or revelator detected the fraud.

Hofmann feared exposure. In October 1985 he murdered Steve Christensen and Kathy Sheets with pipe bombs. The forensic examiner George Throckmorton then proved the documents were forgeries. The church's own history-topics essay now tells the story.

FAIR says discernment is not omniscience. God does not shield leaders from ordinary deception, and Scripture shows prophets being deceived in mundane things. The country's best document examiners, dealers and historians were fooled too. The church bought documents as any archive does, published several of them — including the salamander letter — rather than hiding them, and cooperated with prosecutors. Hofmann's success says something about forgery, and nothing about revelation.

They admit the sequence, and only its meaning is argued. The omniscience answer has force against a cheap gotcha. But D&C 46:23-27 promises the discerning of spirits precisely so the church is not deceived. And notice what the buying shows. Leaders found a salamander origin story plausible enough to acquire and hold.
"D&C 46 promises discernment so the church isn't deceived. How did Hofmann get so far?"

burning-in-bosom-epistemology.t: How the whole system is entered
burning-in-bosom-epistemology.d: Moroni 10:4-5. Pray about the Book of Mormon, and the Holy Ghost will confirm that it is true. It is experienced as a feeling — the burning in the bosom of D&C 9:8. Dallin Oaks describes it as a feeling of comfort and serenity. Alma 32:27-28 sets up the same experiment.
Everything. Members are taught this witness outranks outside evidence. Once confirmed, it validates the whole chain: the book, the prophet, the priesthood, the church.

The method cannot tell things apart. Muslims report it. Catholics report it. Evangelicals report it. So do Strangites, who follow a rival successor to Joseph Smith. The claims contradict each other, so at most one set of feelings is tracking truth.

Scripture puts the test the other way round. Deuteronomy 13:1-3 says reject a prophet whose doctrine is false, even if his sign comes to pass. 1 John 4:1 says "try the spirits." Isaiah 8:20 says "to the law and to the testimony." The Bereans in Acts 17:11 "searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so." And Jeremiah 17:9 says the heart is deceitful above all things.

FAIR argues that personal revelation is thoroughly biblical. James 1:5 says ask of God. Hearts burned on the Emmaus road in Luke 24:32. Peter's testimony came "not by flesh and blood" in Matthew 16:17. The witness is knowledge borne by the Spirit, not raw emotion, and D&C 9:8 commands study first, so feeling confirms work rather than replacing it. Other faiths having spiritual experiences is expected, since God gives light to all. And critics who reduce every spiritual experience to brain chemistry prove too much, because that would undo Christian conversion too.
"A Muslim prays and feels the same certainty. How would either of you tell?"

chiasmus-alma-36.d: A shape in writing. Ideas run out and then back again in reverse — A, B, C, then C, B, A. It turns on a centre. Old Hebrew writers used it, and so does the Bible; Genesis 9:6 and Amos 5:4-6 are examples.

In 1969 John Welch found extended chiasmus in the Book of Mormon. Alma 36 is the showpiece. The whole chapter is laid out that way, turning on the words "born of God." Welch argues Joseph Smith could not have known the form.

Earl Wunderli published it in Dialogue in 2005. He says the outline depends on choosing. Some repeated words are counted as structure; others that break the pattern are not. Chunks of text are skipped. Loose matches are allowed. By Welch's own fifteen criteria, the chapter scores poorly. Chiasm-like shapes also turn up in the Doctrine and Covenants, and in ordinary writing of the 1800s.

Two physicists, Boyd and Farrell Edwards, replied with statistics. They estimate it is very unlikely that Alma 36's repeated elements would fall into that order by chance. Their method, they argue, does not rest on anyone's literary judgement. Apologists add that the shape fits the meaning, with conversion at the centre of an inverted life. They say the candidates in the D&C are weaker. And no evidence puts John Jebb's 1820 book on chiasmus, or any such work, in Joseph Smith's hands.

Genuinely arguable, and this is a real scholarly exchange in peer-reviewed journals. Concede the pattern; contest what follows from it. Even a deliberate chiasm does not prove antiquity. A writer soaked in King James parallelism could produce one, and modern texts contain them. Grant it gracefully and go back to the anachronisms and the DNA.
"I'll grant you the chiasm. Does a shape on the page make a book ancient?"

nahom-nhm-altars.d: 1 Nephi 16:34 says Ishmael was buried "in the place which was called Nahom." Note the wording. The party did not name it; they found it named. Then, at 1 Nephi 17:1, they turn "nearly eastward."

Three limestone altars from the Bar'an temple near Marib, in Yemen, found from 1988 onward. Each carries a dedication by a donor of the NHM tribe, the Nihm. They date to roughly the 600s or 500s BC — Lehi's era. And the Nihm region sits near where the frankincense trail bends east toward the coast.

Warren Aston and Scripture Central call this a precise external hit. NHM is rare as an Arabian place name. The altars anchor the tribal name to exactly Lehi's period and region. Nobody in 1820s New York could have known that. And they stress the chain. A burial place carrying a root that means mourning. Sitting exactly where the text turns east. Ending at plausible candidates for Bountiful on the Omani coast. Each link, they say, multiplies against coincidence.

The inscriptions give three consonants naming a tribe, not a place called Nahom. The NHM root is common in Semitic names. The eastward turn follows the trade route everyone used. And a form of the name, Nehhm, appears on European maps from Carsten Niebuhr's expedition, in English by 1792. Archaeologists outside the church see nothing in it; Philip Jenkins wrote that "there's no there there."

Genuinely arguable, and be honest: this is their best single piece of evidence. A real inscription, correctly dated, plausibly placed. Give it its full weight before you answer. Then note the scale. One consonant cluster in Arabia does not offset an empty New World, where a thousand years of the story take place.
"Nahom is a real hit and I'll say so. What have we found in the Americas?"

succession-crisis.d: Joseph Smith was killed in June, leaving no clear plan for who followed. The movement split. Sidney Rigdon, his counselor. The Quorum of the Twelve under Brigham Young. And James Strang, who produced a letter of appointment dated June 1844 — now at Yale's Beinecke Library, catalogued as attributed.

Strang then dug up his own metal plates at Voree, Wisconsin, in 1845, before four witnesses. There is no direct contemporary evidence that those witnesses ever took it back. That complicates any appeal to the Book of Mormon witnesses.

The people who knew Joseph best. His widow Emma stayed in Nauvoo and married Lewis Bidamon, who was not a Mormon. His mother Lucy and his brother William never gathered to Utah. His son Joseph Smith III became prophet of the rival RLDS church at Amboy, Illinois, in 1860. And none of the Three Witnesses went west in 1847. All had been excommunicated by 1838. Oliver Cowdery was rebaptised in 1848 but died before reaching Utah. Martin Harris came only in 1870. David Whitmer never returned.

succession-crisis.t: What Emma said to the end
succession-crisis.d: In her Last Testimony, printed in the Saints' Herald on 1 October 1879, she denied that Joseph practised polygamy. "He had no other wife but me."

That succession never depended on family. Joseph conferred the keys of the kingdom on the Quorum of the Twelve before he died. On 8 August 1844 the great majority of Nauvoo Saints sustained the Twelve over Rigdon. Strang's letter is judged a forgery on handwriting and postal grounds. Apologists say several Voree witnesses later distanced themselves. On Emma, FAIR argues the documents contradict her, including sealing records from 1843. Her denials are explained four ways. She wanted to protect her sons. She hated polygamy. She was in property disputes with Brigham Young. And she was loyal to the church her son led. Proximity to a prophet, they note, is not the biblical test of truth.
"Why didn't his mother, his widow or his son follow Brigham Young?"

second-anointing.d: An ordinance above the endowment that most members have never heard of. In it a couple's calling and election is made sure, and exaltation is sealed upon them. D&C 131:5 calls that "the more sure word of prophecy." D&C 132:49 stands behind it too. It has been given since 28 September 1843, by invitation of the First Presidency only.

David John Buerger's study in Dialogue in 1983 documents thousands performed in the nineteenth century. Then a sharp cutback, and near-total silence in the twentieth. The church stopped publishing figures by the 1930s.

Mormonr, an apologetic site, states that the ordinance exists, that it is by invitation, and that it "isn't generally taught in Church meetings or in Church publications." It also states that teachers are instructed not to discuss it or answer questions about it.
In 2012. Tom Phillips, a former stake president, received the rite from the apostle M. Russell Ballard. He published a detailed firsthand account and told his story on Mormon Stories.

They do not deny it exists; they defend its privacy. Mormonr calls it sacred rather than secret, handled like other temple matters. There is biblical precedent for anointing individuals, since priests and kings were anointed, and Jesus spoke of mysteries given to some and not others. The blessing is conditional, not a guarantee, so it does not remove the need to endure faithfully. The rarity is prudence. And ordinary members lose nothing, because the same blessings are held out to all, and ordinances missed in this life may be received later.

They do not deny it exists. They defend its privacy. Mormonr calls it sacred rather than secret, handled like other temple matters. There is biblical precedent for anointing people; priests and kings were anointed. Jesus spoke of mysteries given to some and not others. The blessing is conditional, not a guarantee, so it does not remove the need to endure. The rarity is prudence. And ordinary members lose nothing. The same blessings are held out to all, and ordinances missed in this life may be received later.

jst-whole-bible.d: From June 1830 to July 1833 he produced an inspired revision of the whole Bible. He altered roughly 3,400 verses, with no manuscript support for the changes. Then he declared it done. History of the Church, 2 July 1833: "We this day finished the translating of the Scriptures."
D&C 73:4 commanded the work be finished. D&C 124:89 commanded that it be published.

jst-whole-bible.t: What the church did with it
jst-whole-bible.d: Never adopted it. The official Bible is still the King James Version, with a few readings in footnotes and an appendix. The rival RLDS church, now Community of Christ, published the full text in 1867, as the Inspired Version. It held the manuscripts for 150 years. The church bought them in March 2024, with the marked Bible and the Kirtland Temple, in a deal worth $192.5 million.

BYU's own scholars grant that the 1830 Book of Mormon was used as a source for some of the changes to Isaiah. Yet many Book of Mormon readings never made it into the revision, and some were changed again. So he revised verses that his own earlier scripture quotes in the King James form.

FAIR and BYU scholars say the 1833 statement marked the end of a first pass, not a finished book. Joseph kept revising until 1844, and never prepared a manuscript for the press. The command in D&C 124:89 went unfulfilled amid poverty and persecution, so the church inherited a working draft.
