They add that the revision was never meant as a uniform restoration of lost text; it blends restoration, prophetic comment, harmonising and modernising. That explains the differences. And hundreds of its readings went into the footnotes and appendix of the 1979 edition, while the 2024 purchase shows reverence rather than embarrassment.
"If God had him correct the Bible, why does your church still hand out the uncorrected one?"

lectures-on-faith-decanonized.d: Seven Lectures on Faith. In August 1835 a general assembly of the church voted to canonise them as the Doctrine half of the Doctrine and Covenants. That is why the book has that name. They were printed as scripture for 86 years.

A committee removed them. There was no revelation, and no vote of common consent. The explanation given was that they "were never presented to nor accepted by the Church as being otherwise than theological lectures." The 1835 minutes say otherwise; the assembly accepted the whole volume.

Lecture 5 teaches that the Father is "a personage of spirit." That cannot be squared with D&C 130:22, where the Father has a body of flesh and bones. When the doctrine of God changed, the canon was trimmed to match.

FAIR, and Joseph Fielding Smith, who sat on the 1921 committee, argue that the Lectures were lessons and not revelations. They were never claimed as the word of the Lord. They were incomplete on the Godhead. And they were removed to stop members confusing them with actual revelations. On this reading 1921 was housekeeping, not de-canonisation.

They admit this themselves, and the answer concedes the key facts. The 1835 assembly voted to accept the whole book as the doctrine and covenants of their faith, which the 1921 explanation contradicts. And incomplete on the Godhead is a polite way of saying superseded. This pairs with D&C 132, which stays in the canon while being disavowed. One question does the work.
"What revelation removed the Lectures on Faith from your scriptures?"

independence-temple-lot-ownership.d: D&C 57, from 1831, named Independence, Missouri as the "center place" of Zion, and marked the spot for a temple. D&C 84 said the temple would be reared there. D&C 97:19 speaks of it too.

No temple. And the church does not own the dedicated spot. It belongs to the Church of Christ (Temple Lot), a small Hedrickite body of roughly 7,000 members worldwide. They reject Brigham Young, the endowment, and most Latter-day Saint distinctives. They kept the lot through the litigation of the 1890s, and they keep a modest meetinghouse on it.
The 17-million-member church whose canon prophesies that temple. It owns the visitors' centre.

That the temple will still be built, in the Lord's timing. D&C 124:49 says that when enemies prevent a commanded work, God no longer requires it of that generation. The church's own question-and-answer page affirms belief in a future temple in Zion, and notes cordial relations with the Temple Lot church.

They admit the ownership; nobody disputes it. The D&C 124:49 clause cannot explain the present. Nothing stops the church building in Jackson County today, except that it does not own the spot. The owners will not sell, and have refused offers for over a century. Do not argue the dating here. That belongs with the failed-prophecies case, and it should not be counted twice.
"Who owns the temple lot in Independence? It takes five minutes to check."

zions-camp-dc105-reversal.d: D&C 103, from February 1834. Zion — Jackson County — would be redeemed "by power," with the Lord going before the armed expedition. "I will fight your battles." Verses 15-20 say his angels would go up before them.
Zion's Camp marched roughly 900 miles. Cholera killed about a dozen members. Missouri's governor declined to help. No land was recovered.

D&C 105, in June 1834, called it off. The Saints must "wait for a little season for the redemption of Zion." The failure is attributed to their own transgressions. Both the promise and the retraction sit in the canon today. And 192 years later the little season continues.

That D&C 103 was conditional all along. D&C 105 itself says the Saints failed to consecrate and were not ready, so the Lord deferred rather than broke his word. And Zion's Camp is read as a refining trial. Many future apostles and seventies were chosen from among its veterans, so the march succeeded at its real purpose.

Strong for you, and it is unusually clean. The conditions were announced after the failure, not before it. D&C 103 reads as an unconditional promise with angels going ahead. And the refining-trial reading concedes that the stated objective failed. Best of all, you need no outside source. Both halves are in their own scriptures.
"D&C 103 promises Zion. D&C 105 postpones it. How long is a little season?"

one-mighty-and-strong.d: D&C 85:7 promises that God will send "one mighty and strong, holding the scepter of power in his hand," to set in order the house of God. Verse 8 goes with it.

Claimants. A Dialogue survey documents about eighteen main ones. By 1905 at least eight men had already declared themselves. Founders of fundamentalist sects have claimed the title, and so have violent figures, including the LeBaron family.

By press release. In November 1905 the First Presidency published a statement in the Deseret News. It reinterpreted the verse. It was about Bishop Edward Partridge, and land inheritances in the 1830s. And anyone claiming the title, it said, shows great ignorance of God and of the order of the church.

That the 1905 statement is right. The verse concerned the specific situation of Edward Partridge in 1832, and land in Zion. It was likely mooted by Partridge's repentance. Church materials treat the matter as settled by that statement.

Genuinely arguable, and this is a small one. Do not lead with it. The interesting part is the 1905 statement itself. For 73 years the verse sat open and bred claimants, until the First Presidency closed a canonised prophecy by reinterpreting it in a newspaper. That is an act of authority, not a reading members could have reached from the text. It is most useful when fundamentalist offshoots come up.
"Who is the one mighty and strong? Every splinter prophet has claimed that verse."

evolution-shifting-statements.d: The First Presidency published The Origin of Man. It declared Adam "the first man of all men" and dismissed human evolution as "theories of men." The 1925 restatement quietly softened that.

For decades, in public. Joseph Fielding Smith and Bruce R. McConkie condemned evolution as heresy, incompatible with the Fall. James E. Talmage and B. H. Roberts accepted life before Adam. All of them held the same office.
The church's official position is that it has no official position. BYU teaches evolution as settled science.

evolution-shifting-statements.t: What is still in the canon
evolution-shifting-statements.d: No death before the Fall — 2 Nephi 2:22 and Alma 12:23-24. Moses 3:7 calls Adam "the first flesh upon the earth." D&C 77:6-7 gives the earth a temporal history of 7,000 years. The church no longer defends those claims. It has never corrected them either.

Genuinely arguable, and do not overstate it. Never say the church banned evolution; it never quite did, and the neutral framing has real support. The solid core is narrower. Apostles taught flatly contradictory answers to a factual question for seventy years, all claiming prophetic authority. The scientists settled it, and the church followed. Use it as corroboration, not as your lead.
"Which apostle was speaking as a prophet — Talmage or Joseph Fielding Smith?"

mormon-name-reversal.d: Between August and October, President Russell M. Nelson declared that using Mormon or LDS for the church "is a major victory for Satan" and an offence to Jesus. He mandated the full name. The Mormon Tabernacle Choir, LDS.org and mormon.org were all renamed.

mormon-name-reversal.t: What the church had just been doing
mormon-name-reversal.d: The I'm a Mormon advertising campaign, from 2010 to 2018, at a cost of millions. The feature film Meet the Mormons, in 2014. And official pages calling Mormon an inoffensive nickname.

Gordon B. Hinckley, as prophet, embraced the word in public. "Mormon means more good." That was General Conference in October 1990 — answering the plea for the full name that then-Elder Nelson had made earlier that same year.

That the Lord named the church in D&C 115:4, and restoring the full name honours Christ. See also 3 Nephi 27:7-8. The earlier nickname campaigns were well-meant accommodations to public awareness. And prophets can receive updated direction, line upon line, without their predecessors being condemned. Nelson said it was "not a name change… it is a correction" commanded by the Lord.

They admit every fact, and this is a soft one doctrinally. Keep it light. Its use is that it is small, recent, and always coming up. A prophet framed a reversal of his predecessors' public position as timeless divine will, and attached the word Satan to what the church itself did until that year.
"Why can't we say Mormon anymore? Your church was running 'I'm a Mormon' ads until 2018."
